title: Stokes would love to coach England in future
description: Ben Stokes says he would love to become England head coach in the future, as he expresses concerns about the toll captaincy could take on Joe Root.
fullText:
Former England captain Ben Stokes says he would love to become coach of the national team in the future.

The 35-year-old, speaking on the For the Love of Cricket podcast, also expressed surprise at Harry Brook not succeeding him as England Test captain and concern for Joe Root being appointed to the role.

Stokes, who had been England's Test captain since 2022, announced his shock retirement from international cricket in June - during the third and final Test of the series against New Zealand.

The all-rounder's departure came weeks after he missed England's second Test against the Kiwis following an incident in a London nightclub.

"I'm doing my level three coaching now while I'm still playing, because I want, when the day comes that I'm not playing any more, I'd love to be able to have all that stuff signed off and done," said Stokes.

"I know what I want to do in terms of staying within the game, which is to be a coach. And would I love to be coach of England one day? Absolutely.

"I just really like the idea of being, again, like, in some form of leadership away from playing."

Fleming new England Test coach with Root captain

Root in 'very different place' over Test captaincy

Stokes return would not surprise England chief Key

England were beaten 2-1 by New Zealand and the series defeat followed the 4-1 Ashes loss in Australia, meaning they have not won a Test series since late 2024.

Stokes has rejected suggestions he could reverse his England retirement for the 2027 Ashes and, when asked by former team-mate Jos Buttler whether he had definitely retired, Stokes said: "Definitely".

England have since appointed Root as England Test captain instead of fellow batter Brook.

Brook was promoted to Stokes' vice-captain in the Test side for last winter's Ashes tour.

However, he was involved in an off-field controversy in Wellington when he was struck by a bouncer the night before a white-ball game in New Zealand in November.

Root was given the Test captaincy for the second Test against New Zealand, which Stokes missed, and has now been given the role permanently.

Stokes had backed Brook, who leads the white-ball sides, to succeed him in the role.

"I think just if you think someone's going to be a good captain or a good leader, then just give them it," said Stokes.

"I understood the reasoning but I was still like, well, what message is that sending to him?

"He's vice-captain. And then the captain is not playing, but he's not captain. What?"

Root's first spell as Test captain was between 2017 and 2022 and he captained England to a record 27 Test wins in 65 matches.

He will work with new England Test coach Stephen Fleming, the former New Zealand captain, in the role.

Root stepped down from his first stint as skipper in April 2022, following a 10-wicket defeat by West Indies.

At that time, England had won just one of their past 17 Tests, including a 4-0 Ashes humbling in Australia, while also navigating Covid restrictions - with Root saying the job "took its toll" on his health.

"I wish him [Root] nothing but success. I hope he goes on and achieves amazing things in his role as captain and I think he's going to really enjoy it with Flem [Fleming]. He's a great man," said Stokes.

"I've worked with Flem before but I told Joe, I said my only worry is just you. And that's all I really care about now, just because I have seen what he went through and how much he put himself through for someone.

"He's just always put the team first - he always comes second. And that's just my only concern with it, is just obviously knowing what he went through last time he was in charge of the team. I don't want to see that ever happen again because I care for Joe a lot, but I wish him all the success in the world.

"I'm sure he's going to do great. So I'm looking forward to seeing what the team does going forward."

Fleming replaced Brendon McCullum as coach of England's Test team.

McCullum was fired following a string of poor results and several off-field incidents involving his players, but remains in charge of England's white-ball sides.

There were rumours of a rift between him and Stokes during the latter stages of their time together for England, but both have denied that was the case.

McCullum said he told his former captain that he considered him a "good friend", while Stokes said the pair are "mates".

"We never once fell out," said Stokes.

"Did we have discussions with each other that we had different views on and different opinions on? 100% and we both admit that. I think Baz has even said that himself.

"Did we have a fallout? Absolutely not."

title: Rodri unmoved by Barcelona interest as Real Madrid remains his priority
description: According to AS, Real Madrid  target Rodri has made his position clear regarding his future. With just one year remaining on his Manchester City contract, the Spanish midfielder has attracted interest...
fullText:
According to AS, Real Madrid target Rodri has made his position clear regarding his future.

With just one year remaining on his Manchester City contract, the Spanish midfielder has attracted interest from several of Europe's biggest clubs, including Paris Saint-Germain, Bayern Munich, and most recently Barcelona.

However, his preference is said to be unchanged.

According to the report, Rodri has no interest in joining Barcelona or any another club if he leaves Manchester City.

His priority is to return to La Liga, specifically with Real Madrid. That desire, combined with his impressive performances at the World Cup and José Mourinho's approval, has led Madrid to seriously explore a move for the 30-year-old midfielder.

Rodri only wants Real Madrid. (Photo by Angel Martinez/Getty Images)

Barcelona have made an initial approach to assess Rodri's situation following Frenkie de Jong's injury. However, the Catalan club is understood to be aware that the midfielder's priority is Real Madrid.

Even beyond the player's preference, Barcelona face significant financial obstacles.

The club's immediate priorities remain completing deals for Joao Cancelo and a new striker following Robert Lewandowski's departure.

After already investing heavily in Anthony Gordon, Karim Adeyemi, and Jesse Bisiwu, committing another €75 million for Rodri would be extremely difficult.

Other interested clubs, including PSG and Bayern Munich, are also believed to have cooled their pursuit after recognizing the player's preferred destination.

Asking price remains a sticking point. (Photo by Michael Steele/Getty Images)

Real Madrid remain optimistic but cautious about completing the transfer.

Manchester City are asking for around €75 million, while the Merengues hope negotiations can bring the fee closer to €60 million.

To complete the signing, the Spanish club would likely need to sell at least one player, as only one first-team squad place remains available and Yan Diomande is also expected to join.

As speculation continues, Rodri is enjoying his post-World Cup break while recovering from a minor back procedure.

But as far as his future is concerned, the Spain captain is clear: only Real Madrid and nothing else, with an agreement over personal terms already understood to be sorted.

title: Today’s Papers: Milan mourns Baresi, Leão U-turn and Inter close on Romero
description: Italian football pauses on Tuesday to say goodbye to Franco Baresi, and the country’s three sports dailies devote their front pages both to his funeral and to a transfer market showing no sign of sl...
fullText:
Italian football pauses on Tuesday to say goodbye to Franco Baresi, and the country's three sports dailies devote their front pages both to his funeral and to a transfer market showing no sign of slowing.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, Corriere dello Sport and Tuttosport alike, the day belongs to Baresi.

His funeral takes place at 11am at Milan's Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio, where thousands of supporters are expected.

Under headlines including "Per sempre libero" and "Tutto il mondo per salutare Baresi," the papers report that former team-mates from Paolo Maldini and Marco van Basten to Dejan Savićević and Roberto Donadoni will join Milan owner Gerry Cardinale, president Paolo Scaroni and Inter counterpart Beppe Marotta, with delegations from Real Madrid and Barcelona also present.

Milan's first team, on tour in Australia, will be represented only by the injured Christian Pulisic and Santiago Giménez, and will wear black armbands for Wednesday's friendly against Inter in Perth.

The market, though, presses on.

Gazzetta leads with "Giravolta Leao," reporting that Rafael Leão's expected Milan exit is no longer certain: with no concrete offers arriving, the Portugal forward is now working to stay and win back his place under Rúben Amorim.

The pink paper also trumpets Juventus's spending, already €138m, it notes, on the likes of Kerim Alajbegović and Randal Kolo Muani, and Como's capture of Chelsea's Trevoh Chalobah, billed as "another Champions-level signing."

Corriere dello Sport leads on a goalkeeping tangle it dubs "Intrigo Suzuki," with Parma's Zion Suzuki courted by PSG and Juventus exploring a loan move for a keeper as Luciano Spalletti also eyes Guglielmo Vicario.

Its main splash, though, is Cristian Romero: Tottenham are said to be willing to let the Argentine leave for €40m, but his salary and the need for an Inter sale first complicate a deal that Piero Ausilio continues to push.

Tuttosport frames Juventus's attacking business as a "last call," reporting talks with Atlético Madrid over a possible exchange involving Alexander Sørloth and Nico González, the Norwegian said to be ready for Italy, the Argentine keen to stay in Spain.

The Turin paper agrees Inter's pursuit of Romero, alongside Moussa Diaby, is well advanced, declaring the "Cuti" deal all but done.

Off the pitch, Corriere tracks FIFA's fallout: with UEFA threatening legal action after the abandoned World Cup sell-off, it reports that Gianni Infantino has turned to his ally Donald Trump for support, while Concacaf's Victor Montagliani is floated as a possible successor.

title: Kyle Juszczyk: Deebo Samuel is the best, incredible teammate, excited to have him back
description: "His first day in pads he's making an impact right way. He just looked like the old Deebo," Juszczyk said.
fullText:
After one year in Washington, wide receiver Deebo Samuel has returned to San Francisco. And 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk couldn't be happier about that.

Juszczyk, who was in San Francisco for all six of Samuel's seasons on the 49ers, said that Samuel was a great teammate in the past and is already showing that he's a great teammate again.

"Deebo's the best. He's such an incredible teammate. He's such a good friend. He's an incredible football player," Juszczyk said. "So we're really happy to have him in the locker room just because he brings the best vibes, and positivity, but we're also happy to have him on the field because he's still got juice and he can still go out there and make big plays. He came in, he looks like he's in phenomenal shape. His first day in pads he's making an impact right way. He just looked like the old Deebo, so I can't say enough positive things about how excited we are to have him."

The 49ers traded Samuel to the Commanders last year, and when he returned to the 49ers last week, he said it felt like he never left. Juszczyk agrees.

title: Pete Crow-Armstrong details why he likes the ‘Babe Ruth never existed’ conspiracy theory
description: PCA is having a wildly remarkable season for the Chicago Cubs, but a theory he shared recently might be the craziest thing about his year so far. One of the things that makes baseball so wonderful is the immense history associated with the game.
fullText:
PCA is having a wildly remarkable season for the Chicago Cubs, but a theory he shared recently might be the craziest thing about his year so far.

One of the things that makes baseball so wonderful is the immense history associated with the game. Professional baseball has been around almost 160 years, with many legendary figures along the way.

Perhaps no player in the game's history is as storied as Babe Ruth. One of the most popular Americans in history, the 7-time World Series winner is a mythological figure within the sport.

While most fans think of him with reverence, there are theories that suggest his achievements were over-exaggerated. And now Chicago Cubs star Pete Crow-Armstrong has shared one that goes even farther.

Crow-Armstrong had a historic run through June and July of 2026. In 195 ABs combined, PCA posted a .333 batting average while hitting 17 homers and notching 37 RBIs.

In a recent podcast appearance on Let's Be Honest with Kristin Cavallari, the Cubs man was asked to share his craziest conspiracy theory, which is when he shared his wild take about the baseball legend.

"Babe Ruth never existed is one that I really like," Crow-Armstrong said when asked about his favourite theories. "Some pitcher with the Mariners… Salcedo?

"I think he did some podcast on Zoom when he was like, going down the rabbit hole with somebody of 'Babe Ruth never existed.' And I was like, 'Dude, that's awesome.'

"We always talk about how the game's evolving. And people might as well have underhanding the ball to that guy and we talk about him as one of the greatest players ever. Might as well dive further into it and be like, 'Maybe he never existed.'"

PCA has been known to say things that are a little outlandish, but this is wild even for him. Considering that he is in the running for NL MVP, he might want to tone down the conspiracy theories.

title: Ferran on his MEGA cap: "Honestly, I know nothing about politics"
description: Barcelona striker, who may change clubs next season, told CNN his presence on Spain's victory parade at Cibeles in a cap echoing Trump's slogan was no big deal.View on euronews
fullText:
'Make America Great Again' (MAGA). The slogan, copied and reworked ad nauseam, even by groups hardly suspected of sharing Trumpist ideas, does not seem to have taken its toll on the Valencian Ferran Torres, who showed off a similar cap during the celebrations for La Roja's World Cup victories.

"It was just to have fun with my friends and family and it had nothing to do with politics," Torres said in English during an interview with 'CNN' after being asked about the initials on the cap, reworked as 'Make Spain Great Again'. "Honestly, I don't know anything about politics. It was only about being able to see Spain back on top again, winning the Cup."

The Trump administration, however, interpreted the forward's gesture as tacit support for the MAGA ideology, the populist wing of the Republicans rallying around the president. "Everyone wants to join this movement," the White House's official account even posted, a profile that since Trump's arrival has been used as a media loudspeaker for his circle.

Torres is reportedly in talks to leave Barça ahead of next season, amid rumours he could sign for Paris Saint-Germain, coached by Luis Enrique. CNN journalist Kaitlan Collins asked him directly about his future and PSG. "Right now the only thing I know is that I have to go back there on 12 August and train with them," the player said with a smile. "We'll see what happens (...) in football everything can change in an instant, I'm ready for anything."

The 26-year-old, born in 2000, scored the goal that secured the 2026 World Cup title against Argentina, in the 106th minute of the final played at the New York/New Jersey stadium. A day later, as reports were circulating that Torres owned a property company which had allegedly bought '20 homes in Valencia' to speculate with, he paraded the controversial cap during the victory parade held in Madrid. The player's entourage insisted that the story about the vulture fund was false.

'CNN' has not been the only studio Ferran Torres has appeared on during his stay in the United States, with further interviews scheduled on 'ESPN' and on NBC's Today show.

In recent days, the possibility of signing a new striker has been replaced by the possibility of Ferran Torres leaving the club amid interest from PSG.

The Spanish forward has less than 12 months left on his current deal at the club and is yet to put pen to paper on a new contract.

When asked what needs to happen for him to sign a new contract, Ferran put the onus on Barça to come and show him that they want to keep him.

Now, according to Fabrizio Romano, Barcelona remain determined to keep Ferran, with the club prepared to sanction a departure only under one specific condition.

Ferran's contract expires in 2027. (Photo by Florencia Tan Jun/Getty Images)

Barcelona will only consider Ferran's departure if the player verbally communicates his desire to leave.

Otherwise, the 26-year-old is expected to remain at the club.

Barça continue to view him as an important part of Hansi Flick's project and would only reassess their position if the player himself requested an exit.

Ferran has so far not done that, although he has also not shut down the exit talks once and for all, leaving the door open to all possibilities.

Ferran's words clearly reflected one thing: he wants the Catalan club to show that they care about him and want to keep him beyond 2027.

From his perspective, not being offered a deal yet despite being in the final 12 months of his contract could lead to some insecurities.

Having scored the World Cup-winning goal for Spain, he is at an all-time high in his career, and it is understandable that he wants to make the most of it.

Will Ferran stay or leave? (Photo by David Ramos/Getty Images)

As for Barça, the club are trying to push his renewal talks to September to accommodate them after the new La Liga season begins.

Barcelona's position is becoming increasingly clear.

The club do not want to lose Ferran this summer and still see him as an important member of Flick's squad, particularly following Robert Lewandowski's departure.

However, their actions towards the player must also reflect that stance. Barça also cannot afford to let his situation drag on until late in the window.

For now, both parties appear willing to continue together, subject to talks about the future, but the next step will be decisive.

If Barcelona open formal renewal talks and convince Ferran that he remains central to the project, all this exit talk can come to an end.

If not, PSG will continue knocking on the door until they eventually burst it open.

title: Van Gaal says he's open for a fourth coaching spell at Netherlands
description: Louis van Gaal said that he's open for a fourth coaching spell at the Netherlands national team. "I always want to help the Dutch Football Federation (KNVB), just as I also wanted to do at Ajax," Van Gaal told the Voetbal International in an interview published on Monday evening.
fullText:
Louis van Gaal said that he's open for a fourth coaching spell at the Netherlands national team.

"I always want to help the Dutch Football Federation (KNVB), just as I also wanted to do at Ajax," Van Gaal told the Voetbal International in an interview published on Monday evening.

"And with such a squad, there are of course possibilities. I also think that the Netherlands could still possibly become European or world champions, because 95% of the squad play abroad and often at good clubs."

Dutch media has suggested the 74-year-old as a potential successor to Ronald Koeman, who resigned following the Netherlands' early exit from the World Cup in North America last month.

Van Gaal said he's astonished with the fact that no ideal successor has been found so far and that coaches such as Arne Slot and Erik ten Hag have turned down the job.

"The only thing going on is that at this moment they still cannot get anyone and then my name comes up again. I find that rather unbelievable," he said.

"Four years ago at the World Cup in Qatar we lost on penalties in the quarter-finals and 'people' did not think our football was good enough. And those people now see me as the ideal man?"

He added that so far he hasn't had talks with the federation.

"I therefore have absolutely no idea what the KNVB wants," he said.

Van Gaal coached the national team in 2000-2001, 2012-2014 and 2021-2022. His best result was finishing in third at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil.

The KNVB will hope to find a new coach soon as their next game is on September 24 against Germany.

title: Bills Get Bad News on Key Defensive Lineman Coming Off Breakout Season
description: Buffalo Bills defensive lineman Deone Walker was hurt in the team's practice on Monday. The post Bills Get Bad News on Key Defensive Lineman Coming Off Breakout Season appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The Buffalo Bills had their first padded practice of training camp on Monday, and didn't get out of it unscathed.

The team has already been dealing with a series of minor injuries, and saw key defensive lineman Deone Walker go down on Monday. Though the extent of the injury was not yet known, it's a blow for a team undergoing some major changes in the offseason.

As reporter Randy Gurzi of SI.com noted, Walker was seen getting medical attention during Monday's practice.

"Deone Walker was a breakout star as a rookie and is expected to take his game to a new level under Jim Leonhard," Gurzi wrote. "Unfortunately, we didn't get to see him in action when the pads came on. Instead, Walker was seen working with the trainers on the sideline, and while there was no update on what happened, a sleeve on his left arm suggests that's where he was injured."

Reporter Alex Brasky noted that the Bills had a surprising replacement ready, with former practice squad member Phidarian Mathis taking snaps in his place and not former third-round pick DeWayne Carter.

"Phidarian Mathis was first in line to replace the injured Deone Walker on Monday at Bills training camp Mathis quietly had a good year in 2025 despite seeing limited action," Brasky wrote on X. "Mathis over DeWayne Carter, who made the move inside to nose tackle, is an interesting development"

There is no indication that Walker could be dealing with a long-term injury, and he could be headed to a significant role with the team. The Bills are shifting to a new 3-4 base defense under defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard, who said this spring that Walker could play nose tackle.

Leonhard also mentioned Carter as a potential nose tackle candidate, noting that each player could be asked to play the role a bit differently.

"Right now, there's a number of players that we're repping in that position," Leonhard said, via the team's official website. "Whether you're a zero, a shade â the techniques that you can use â there's a lot of different ways to get it done. And it might be a little bit on an individual basis on who's in there and what we're going to ask them to do."

Leonhard added that the new scheme could unlock defensive tackle Ed Oliver, who appeared headed for an All-Pro season in 2025 before losing a long stretch due to injury.

"I think Ed's going to be really disruptive in this defense," Leonhard said. "The base defense being more different for him than what it's been in the past, and in all reality, a little bit more freedom than he's had in the past. The sub package things are a little bit more familiar to what they've done here from a front structure."

Leonhard added that he would be taking a more aggressive approach to putting pressure on opposing quarterbacks, an area where the Bills often struggled under former head coach Sean McDermott.

title: Sky Sports: Liverpool to miss out on transfer targe as rivals reach agreement
description: Ayyoub Bouaddi to Manchester City latest leaves Liverpool weighing Trey Nyoni optionManchester City are moving into a strong position in the race for Ayyoub Bouaddi, with Sky Sports reporter Florian P...
fullText:
Manchester City are moving into a strong position in the race for Ayyoub Bouaddi, with Sky Sports reporter Florian Plettenberg reporting that the Lille midfielder "has reached a full verbal agreement" with the Premier League club. Negotiations with Lille are still continuing, and other sides remain attentive, but the direction of travel appears increasingly clear.

For Liverpool, this looks like one of those situations where admiration and action have not aligned. Bouaddi had been viewed as a player of interest in recruitment circles, yet interest alone does not complete a deal, particularly when the financials begin to escalate. The figures now being discussed around the Moroccan international are significant, with estimates around £85m placing the move firmly into premium territory.

That matters because Liverpool's transfer window cannot be viewed through one signing in isolation. Squad planning under Andoni Iraola requires balance, and there are multiple areas still under assessment before the new campaign begins. Committing that level of outlay to one midfield addition would inevitably shape the rest of the summer, especially if Liverpool are also exploring other high-cost attacking options such as Bradley Barcola.

From a recruitment perspective, there is logic in stepping back when valuations move beyond a club's comfort zone. Bouaddi is highly regarded and clearly attracting major interest, but Liverpool do not appear prepared to be dragged into an inflated battle if it compromises wider business. That is a strategic call, not necessarily a reflection on the player.

Timing is also important here. Liverpool have spent pre-season assessing internal solutions, and Trey Nyoni has done his chances no harm at all. His display against Leeds United offered another reminder of his technical quality and growing authority in midfield. He played a central role in the move that led to Florian Wirtz's goal, switching play superbly to Jeremie Frimpong before the final ball arrived.

Perhaps more telling was the change in Liverpool's midfield after Nyoni went off at half-time. The structure looked less secure and the fluency dipped, which only added weight to the impression he is becoming a serious option in Iraola's plans. That does not mean he and Bouaddi are direct comparisons, but it does strengthen the case for trusting what is already emerging at Kirkby.

If Liverpool are working within tighter financial parameters than in previous windows, decisions like this become easier to understand. Passing on an £85m midfielder may create room to address several needs rather than one. Bouaddi may yet prove worth every penny at Manchester City, but Liverpool's approach suggests they are prioritising flexibility, value and squad-wide improvement over a headline purchase.

In that context, Nyoni's rise could become more than a promising subplot. It may help shape the whole window.

As a disappointed Liverpool supporter, this report is frustrating even if it makes sense on paper. Bouaddi looks like exactly the sort of elite young midfielder top clubs should be fighting for, and hearing that Manchester City are close to getting him while Liverpool stand aside never sits well. Supporters can accept missing out on a player, but it becomes harder to take when a direct rival appears ready to strengthen without the same hesitation.

There is a wider concern too. Liverpool cannot keep leaning on the idea that internal development will solve every squad issue. Trey Nyoni has looked excellent and deserves enormous credit, but expecting a 19-year-old to carry such responsibility across a long season feels unfair. Young players should be supported, not used as the reason to avoid major investment.

If the price really is around £85m, then caution is understandable. Still, elite midfielders cost elite money, and Liverpool know that better than most. The concern from a fan perspective is that this starts to look like another summer of careful explanations rather than decisive action. Bouaddi may have been expensive, but watching Manchester City add another top talent while Liverpool talk themselves out of it is difficult to dress up as anything other than a disappointment.

fullText:
After weeks of speculations and delays, AFC Ajax have announced the signing of FC Barcelona captain Marc-Andre ter Stegen on a season-long loan deal.

"Ajax has reached an agreement with FC Barcelona and Marc ter Stegen. The 34-year-old goalkeeper joins the club on a season-long loan from the Spanish side," their statement read.

Barcelona, too, have confirmed the loan departure of the veteran goalkeeper.

Ter Stegen has been out of favour at Barcelona since last season, following the signing of Joan Garcia as the new No. 1 for Hansi Flick.

The German international left the club on loan in January, signing for Girona, but could only two matches before an injury ruled him out for the rest of the campaign.

Having returned to Barcelona over the summer, Ter Stegen started pre-season under Flick while trying to secure a move away.

An agreement with Ajax had been reached for a while now, with the goalkeeper reuniting with former Girona manager Michel.

But there were delays in the move going through due to tax-related issues. Ultimately, though, a breakthrough was achieved last week, when Ter Stegen was in England with the rest of the Barcelona squad on their pre-season camp.

Loan departure confirmed. (Photo by Eric Alonso/Getty Images)

Ter Stegen flew to Amsterdam on Friday, and completed his medicals on Saturday, with the transfer now finally being announced.

Welcoming the German to the club, Ajax director Jordi Cruyff, formerly of Barcelona, said:

"Marc has an outstanding track record, and his qualities are widely recognized. He is an immediate addition to our squad. Marc and I know each other well, and I'm looking forward to working with him again.

"We have been working on bringing him here for quite some time, so we're very pleased that he has signed his contract and can now get started."

Ajax will bear only a small share of the salary, with Barcelona carrying the majority of his wages for the season.

title: Mason Awe, Three Rivers grad, named Emrick/Mielcarek Male Athlete of the Year
description: Awe excited for opportunity at Kalamazoo College, voted Athlete of the Year
fullText:
THREE RIVERS — Mason Awe knows the overall workload when he arrives at the college level will be a lot.

But he's ready for it. In carrying a solid effort in his time at Three Rivers High School both on the playing field and in the classroom, Awe understands what it will take to be successful.

Now, as he put it, he just has to continue to bring the work ethic on a daily basis. A challenge? Sure. Is he scared? Not gonna happen.

Awe was chosen as the recipient of the 2026 Corky Emrick & Tom Mielcarek Male Athlete of the Year award. The honor, presented by Sturgis Journal Sports Editor Brandon Watson, is a yearly one for a local graduating senior who played multiple sports throughout their high school tenure in addition to being a solid student and a strong member of the community.

Each year, a panel is put together by Watson, and votes are cast for nominated senior student athletes.

"You know, I think I'll miss seeing my friends every day. Coming into school, you know who you are going to see on a daily basis and who will be at school to talk to," Awe said of moving on. "Going to college, everyone will probably be going their own way. They'll each have their own things going on."

Awe will continue his football playing career with Kalamazoo College later this fall. The academic draw was a big one for Awe to Kalamazoo. He has a nice scholarship in his pocket and plans to make the most of it.

The decision, he said, came down to playing football or baseball at the next level.

"It came down to I love playing football, I like playing baseball. So part of the reason I picked K was because I love football," he said. "I could have an opportunity to play baseball there as well, but we will see what happens. Dual sporting is a lot."

The location of the school, its proximity to his home in Three Rivers and facilities were also positive pulls for Kalamazoo and Awe.

"It felt like the right place," he said.

Facing adversity is nothing new for the Three Rivers grad. He missed his entire junior season on the football field with a significant knee injury. But he was determined to get back onto the field of play at all costs and eventually came back to play that junior season for the Wildcat baseball team.

It helped propel him into his senior year on the gridiron.

"I think coming off that injury, getting a chance to play baseball as a junior, it really kept my confidence up going into football that fall," Awe said. "I wasn't being tackled in baseball, but I did a lot of the running and cutting with my legs, so I felt good. It was full-send; I had to trust it."

Awe returned for his senior season and helped lead the Wildcats to the MHSAA football playoffs.

At Kalamazoo, he plans to study either business or economics. Kalamazoo offers a major and minor to its undergraduate students, so Awe will have an option there as well. It could be political science, it might not.

"We're just gonna have to see where it goes," he said.

Growing up, football was everything outside of family for Awe. It even included family as he played for father Jeff in the purple and black. Awe has been throwing a pigskin since he could walk, and with dad being a coach, he was continually around the older players and soaking it all in.

"Summer workouts, always being around the older guys, and I couldn't wait to be in that position, to play on the big field," Awe recalled about being a youngster around the program. "It grew on me a lot. I will miss it, the Friday nights. Walking out those doors, the atmosphere, the band. It's just different."

The Kalamazoo College playbook will certainly be bigger than what Awe is used to. He admitted seeing it already and trying to become acclimated as early as possible. There's a lot to it, obviously, and with him being a future quarterback for the Hornets, he will be expected to know it from cover to end.

"I'll learn it; I'm not worried about that," he said.

The Hornets will open the season at home against Kenyon College (Ohio) at 1 p.m. Sept. 5.

title: Manthey explains Feller struggle in teammate duel: "Same as with Guven"
description: 10-0 in qualifying against Thomas Preining: Ricardo Feller is still struggling to adapt at Manthey, but the Porsche squad sees parallels to DTM champion Guven
fullText:
After five of eight DTM weekends, a clear internal hierarchy has emerged at Porsche top team Manthey. Thomas Preining, who has been with the team since 2022 and became champion in 2023, clearly has the upper hand over newcomer Ricardo Feller, leading the qualifying head-to-head 10-0. Preining also holds a significant lead in the overall standings, sitting in fourth place with 117 points compared to Feller, who is 14th with 64 points.

But how is Manthey handling the fact that Feller, as the successor to champion Ayhancan Guven, has so far been clearly overshadowed by Preining? "We are very satisfied with the development; that was clear to us beforehand," says Patrick Arkenau, who serves as Head of Track Operations at Manthey, when asked by Motorsport-Total.com.

"We dont see anything negative at all; instead, it is progressing exactly as we wished, if not even a little better," the engineer says, backing the Swiss newcomer who has been part of the Porsche roster for just over a year.

But why didnt Manthey expect Feller to challenge Preining right from the start? "It was clear to us - and we know this from previous years - that it is always difficult to enter this environment, also in terms of the way we work," Arkenau explains.

"And of course, racing against Tommy, who is now in his fourth year with Manthey - with the car, with the same key people, with the same key positions - he doesnt have to think about anything. It has become second nature for him," he says, referring to the fact that Preining has been driving for Manthey since the end of 2022 - and not just in the DTM.

"We saw the same thing with Ayhancan in 2024," Arkenau says, pointing to Ayhancan Guven's debut year with Manthey. Guven had a difficult start in 2024, only being able to keep up with Preining from the middle of the season onwards before sensationally becoming DTM champion in 2025.

This is also due to Manthey's way of working. It takes a certain amount of time "until you have fully arrived in this system and can make the most of it for yourself. We are seeing the same thing now with Ricardo. In the end, the DTM is a very special championship - and we follow a relatively special approach. It simply takes time to grow together as a pairing."

And there is something else: The Porsche 911 GT3 R Evo could also play a role, as Feller drove the Audi R8 LMS GT3 until last year and only spent limited time in the Porsche in 2025. While switching to many GT3 cars is not a major hurdle, the agile Porsche with its rear-engine layout requires a specific driving style that many drivers struggle with initially.

Arkenau expects Feller to undergo a similar development to Guven, who first broke into the top three with Manthey at the 2024 season finale in Hockenheim with third place in both qualifying and the race. "We see a very clear upward trend with Ricardo," says Manthey's DTM Head of Track Operations.

"I think we will see the same thing as with Ayhancan, that Ricardo will be absolutely competitive by the end of the season - on a par with Tommy - and then we will go on the full attack again next year with two cars. Exactly as we saw from 2024 to 2025," Arkenau announces.

title: Jason Whitlock claims the WNBA is showing Caitlin Clark how protected she was at Iowa
description: Jason Whitlock has usually defended Caitlin Clark’s presence in the WNBA, but the former ESPN analyst believes she has regressed in recent months. Clark has struggled to an extent during her third season in the WNBA, being outperformed by other emerging stars like Paige Bueckers and her teammate, Kelsey Mitchell.
fullText:
Jason Whitlock has usually defended Caitlin Clark's presence in the WNBA, but the former ESPN analyst believes she has regressed in recent months.

Clark has struggled to an extent during her third season in the WNBA, being outperformed by other emerging stars like Paige Bueckers and her teammate, Kelsey Mitchell.

And Jason Whitlock believes the reason behind her recent issues and behaviour concerns stems from her time at the University of Iowa.

Speaking on his show Fearless, Jason Whitlock suggested that spending her college years playing at Iowa rather than a Division 1 powerhouse team kept Caitlin Clark protected.

Since coming to the WNBA, Clark hasn't realised that she needs to play a scrappier and aggressive brand of basketball, something he believes she never learned at the University of Iowa.

"When I look at Caitlin Clark, she never left Iowa, which protected her from being in practice. She could have went to any of these great schools, and she could have been practising against other elite players.

"She shows up in the WNBA, and she thinks the solution to every problem is, 'Well, let me just shoot more threes, that's how I fixed all the problems.'

"Paige Bueckers, Aliyah Boston, and many of these other players are like, 'No, I got a teammate over here that can fix the problem.'

"'When I'm facing competition that's equal to mine, I don't throw a tantrum, I don't blame the referees, I just compete harder and go to another level and realise this is going to be a dog fight. I'm not going to dominate. It's just going to be an ugly dog fight for the entire afternoon.'

"I don't think she learned that Iowa and some people that are critics, not me, are saying… They look a little lost.

"When the going gets tough, they start throwing tantrums, and they start lobbing up three pointers rather than [saying], 'I got this teammate over here that can handle this. You know what? I'm not going to look to the refs to bail me out. I'm going to bail myself out by playing smarter.'"

There is room to criticise Caitlin Clark for her excessive complaining and lobbying towards the referees since she joined the WNBA.

But to make the suggestion that Clark never had to play a gritty brand of basketball before becoming a professional shows that Whitlock never watched Clark play at the University of Iowa.

In both 2023 and 2024, Clark managed to take the University of Iowa to consecutive NCAA national championship games.

And to get there, they had to get through some of the toughest teams in the country, while Clark navigated her way past tough and physical defences.

To suggest that Clark is a weak-willed and soft player is a ridiculous assertion from Whitlock, who has complimented her presence in the league in years past.

title: From borrowing spikes to India call-up: Auqib Nabi replaces injured Jasprit Bumrah in Test squad for Sri Lanka
description: Jammu and Kashmir bowler Auqib Nabi received his first India Test call-up. He replaces the injured Jasprit Bumrah for the Sri Lanka series. Nabi has been a consistent performer in domestic cricket for years. His impressive Ranji Trophy and India A performances earned him this opportunity. This selection recognises outstanding domestic cricket achievements.
fullText:
MUMBAI: Jammu and Kashmir swing bowler Auqib Nabi was finally rewarded for his consistent performances in domestic cricket on Monday, being named the replacement for the injured Jasprit Bumrah in India's Test squad for the two-match series in Sri Lanka.

The 29-year-old has earned his maiden India call-up and if he makes his Test debut, will become the first cricketer from J&K to play a Test match for India.

It marks a remarkable rise for the Baramulla seamer, who did not even own a pair of bowling spikes when he attended his first under-19 trials and had to borrow them from a friend.

Nabi has taken a staggering 104 wickets across the last two Ranji Trophy seasons, including 60 at an astonishing average of 12.56 in the 2025-26 campaign, when he played a pivotal role in J&K's maiden Ranji Trophy triumph. He also impressed on the recent India 'A' tour of Sri Lanka, claiming six wickets in two fourday matches, including figures of 4-58 in the first innings of the opening game.

Named player of the tournament in the Ranji Trophy, Nabi registered seven five-wicket hauls last season. His standout performances included 5-54 in the final against Karnataka, match figures of 9-123 in the semifinal against Bengal and 12-110 in the quarterfinal against Madhya Pradesh.

Former India allrounder Irfan Pathan believes Nabi has thoroughly earned his opportunity.

"It's not just about last season. Nabi has been performing consistently for a while now and I'm confident he'll do well if he gets an opportunity. Sri Lanka usually offers seamers a bit of assistance, especially in humid conditions," Pathan told TOI.

Pathan also welcomed the selectors rewarding domestic performers such as Nabi and Madhya Pradesh off-spinning allrounder Saransh Jain. "It's recognition for domestic cricket. Test cricket should reward consistent performances in the Ranji Trophy and Duleep Trophy," he said.

Having mentored J& K during his coaching stint, Pathan explained what makes Nabi so effective.

"His action is compact and repeatable, allowing him to hit the seam consistently," Pathan said. "His biggest strength is his seam position. Because it's so upright, the ball moves late after pitching and forces batters to play. That's why he has troubled even top domestic batters."

Pathan also believes Nabi's experience of bowling long spells in first-class cricket will ease his transition to Test cricket. "He bowls long spells regularly, so his body is used to that workload. That's a big advantage. Now it's about making the most of the opportunity." To those questioning Nabi's pace, Pathan offered a blunt response. "How much pace do you want? If you're dismissing batters while bowling in the 130s by making them play defensively, you're doing something right. Control and late movement are what matter."

Former India allrounder Parvez Rasool, the first cricketer from J& K to represent India in international cricket, congratulated Nabi on social media. "What is meant for you will find you. No amount of rejection or ignorance can change your destiny. Heartiest congratulations, Auqib Nabi, on your well-deserved selection to the Indian Test squad."

title: East Bridgewater fighter Joe Lauzon targets comeback at Fenway Park
description: The East Bridgewater High alum, 42, has not appeared in a fight since UFC Fight Night in 2019. His comeback is set at Fenway Park this month.
fullText:
BOSTON — When Joe Lauzon knocked out Jonathan Pierce on UFC Fight Night at TD Garden in 2019, many (including Dana White) thought it made for the perfect finale to his career.

The East Bridgewater High graduate wasn't so certain.

"I said in the cage, 'I'm not saying I'm done, and I'm not saying I'm definitely going to fight again,'" Lauzon said. "But I'm open to opportunities."

Lauzon, 42, is indeed fighting again. He will be featured on the upcoming Bare-knuckle Fighting Championship (BKFC-92) card at Fenway Park on Saturday, Aug. 29, pitted against Stash Kuykendall in the welterweight division.

During a press conference on Tuesday, July 28, Lauzon shut down the mention that he retired.

"Even an old dog with two teeth can still bite," said Abington's Peter 'Slippery Pete' Barrett, who is also featured on the upcoming card. "... Joe's gonna be in this kid's face non-stop, trying to put him out the whole time."

Following his most recent appearance seven years ago, Lauzon trained for a bout against the now-retired Donald 'Cowboy' Cerrone in a marquee UFC lightweight fight in 2022.

Lauzon said both made weight ahead of the first matchup, and Cerrone canceled due to an illness. Then, both made weight for a second time six weeks later, and Lauzon canceled due to a meniscus injury.

Lauzon has had time to rest and recover in the aftermath. He then received a cold call from BKFC executive Rick Caldwell, gauging his interest in participating in the upcoming bare-knuckle card at Fenway, though he has never boxed before, gloves or not.

"I was like, 'If I don't this, I'm going to be upset with myself later,'" Lauzon said. "We've got to roll the dice and see how it goes."

More: Here's what's next for Bridgewater Little League on road to Williamsport

Lauzon owns a 28-15 record in his professional career from 2004-19. He began fighting in the UFC in 2006.

"Joe Lauzon is one of the most popular sports figures in the Boston area and we're very excited for him to make his bare-knuckle debut at our Fenway Park event," BKFC founder and president David Feldman said in a statement.

"The biggest thing was getting back into the groove," Lauzon said of his comeback. "I feel better now physically than I did when I was fighting all of the time because you're always accumulating and collecting injuries. I've had time now to rest."

Lauzon was born in Brockton and moved to East Bridgewater in third grade. He graduated from East Bridgewater High, and now lives in Bridgewater. He owns 'Lauzon Mixed Martial Arts' gyms in Raynham and Canton.

In preparation for the fight at Fenway, Lauzon commuted to Chelmsford multiple times per week to spar with trainer Mike Perry. When asked what the biggest learning curve is with bare-knuckle boxing, Lauzon chuckled and said, "I don't know what I don't know yet. ..."

"I think my style is very good for that because I try to get in really quick, crash and close space as I punch on my way in," he said. "Usually I'm getting in so I can hit a takedown. Now, it's going to be getting into a clinch and fighting in a clinch. ... We'll see how it goes."

Lauzon ranks tied with Dustin Poirier for sixth all-time in UFC Fight Night bonuses with 15.

In his career, he stamped nine wins by knockout and 17 by submission (10th-most in UFC history). Lauzon TKO'd Jonathan Pierce in the span of 1:33 in the first round of his most recent appearance seven years ago, landing 28 strikes compared to Pierce's eight.

After that fight, Dana White said in a press conference that he and Lauzon had a deal that the Pierce matchup would be the finale of Lauzon's career: "What better way to go out than tonight?" White said after the fight at TD Garden in 2019.

"I'm so excited to fight at Fenway," Lauzon said. "I'm excited about the entire thing. It's a great feeling to be fighting at home."

The pedestrians who flee after the tank explodes and huddle at a distance are modelled after the population of Riga: some old, some young, some friendly to Nato, others less so.

But the entire thing is a simulation. It has been built by Skyral, a UK company that is part of a consortium that recently won a £2bn contract from the Ministry of Defence to train the British army.

Modern armies have been training in virtual environments for decades. In 2002, the US army launched a video game called America’s Army, initially run on Windows, a multiplayer shooting scenario that aimed to model combat situations but was criticised as being propaganda for the US military.

A new generation of companies are trying to offer something different: intricate, layered models of systems or places that can capture the second-order consequences of events. Skyral aims to allow militaries to recreate cities and even entire countries. The purpose is less to familiarise a fighter pilot with how to handle an F-16, and more to train soldiers and tacticians on the consequences of a decision.

For example, if a missile strike hits a crowded city street, the population will flee. But if that missile knocks out a power station on a cold winter’s day, the same people are likely to shelter in different areas.

There’s limited research on how much a technology like Skyral’s might improve how soldiers are trained. Broadly, games work: earlier research has suggested that service personnel who have trained on flight simulators perform far better in real-world scenarios. But there are limits to how effectively such scenarios model real-world environments, or how transferable they are to combat. That said, running a simulation is easier and cheaper than organising live combat drills – which is why militaries are spending billions on them. They may not perfectly replicate the real world, but they allow soldiers to train key skills on repeat.

The ideas Skyral is offering have been in development for some time. But the UK will be one of the first militaries to integrate the technology deeply into training its forces. The contract comes amid a wider public debate around how much money the UK is allocating to defence, and if this is sufficient to address changing and growing threats.

How is it different than soldiers playing Call of Duty?

It’s “probably a bit more Fortnite on steroids,” says Naomi Hulme, Skyral’s co-chief executive, who co-founded the company with Jason Kennedy, formerly of the military tech company Raydon. Hulme joined the company after 20 years at BAE Systems, soon after the company was spun from Improbable Worlds Limited, a software company focused on gaming engines and the metaverse.

They began with the virtual worlds that Improbable had developed, Hulme said. “If you swap, like, wizards for soldiers and dragons for tanks, it becomes really sort of defence applicable.” But over time, they built something else: a platform that integrates layers upon layers of information to build, as far as possible, a faithful and usable model of a real city and a real battlefield.

Skyral calls this a “digital twin”. The term originally referred to virtual models of machines, such as cars, that enabled predictive maintenance – for example, by simulating how the brake pads might wear down after five years’ use. But it has widened out recently to refer to new, more ambitious efforts to model reality and allow armies – and humanitarian missions and surgeons – to game out complex decisions.

“It has become a buzzword,” says Wiktor Dotter, the chief executive of Power Size Technologies, a defence and automotive-tech company based in Royal Leamington Spa.

Power Size Technologies is working with the UK military – as well as the US and a few others – on a separate set of simulations. The company builds virtual models of energy systems – everything from the batteries in a tank to the solar panels in a desert camp – and offers these to militaries to help them decide how to electrify their equipment.

These technologies are particularly applicable to the military, he says, where procurement is expensive and decisions are political and take time. It is more challenging to trial a new tank than a new car.

“In defence, you will see quickly that if the development of technology is not connected to usability, so everything’s driven by policy and rules,” he says. “What we try to do is say [to the] MoD: ‘You want to try solar panels in the desert? … You can just do that in simulation. You want to have a crazy idea to have a hybrid battle tank? You can just do it right here in simulation. We have enough data to do that.’”

Skyral’s value proposal is to develop ways to train soldiers on the second-order consequences of battlefield decisions – how combat might affect logistics networks, critical infrastructure, and the behaviour of a human population. To do this, it builds extensive models of real cities, such as Riga.

“In defence, you may well be making decisions without understanding the full consequences,” said Hulme. “What we do in a digital environment is you can test those decisions.”

Meanwhile, a cluster of Nato researchers have been working on digital twins, though often more limited setups, such as models of underwater systems. The difference is in degree. Skyral is offering models that extend far beyond a single system, attempting to incorporate layer upon layer of information: the shape of the electrical grid, and the age and education levels of a real population, for example.

“All of these things that up until now have been done in very siloed sort of modelling – you’re taking all of those models and bringing them all together,” said Hulme. “If you impact one, you see the cascading impact.”

title: Apple launches legal challenge against UK government demand to access data
description:

fullText:
The Home Office has made a fresh request for ‘back door’ access to encrypted iCloud data belonging to British users

Apple has launched a new legal challenge against a UK government demand to access its customers’ highly encrypted data, a year after the Home Office agreed to abandon its previous request.

The US tech company launched the legal complaint last month at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT), an independent court that has the power to investigate claims that the UK intelligence services have acted unlawfully.

The UK government had made a second request to Apple to grant it a “back door” to encrypted iCloud data belonging to British users, according to an order issued by the court.

Britain backed down on its original demand for access to data from UK and US customers last year, after a heated transatlantic tussle over encryption between London and Washington.

UK authorities subsequently issued a new “technical capability notice” (TCN) to Apple that did not apply to American users.

Apple is seeking to challenge the British government’s powers to issue TCNs under the UK Investigatory Powers Act, according to the details of the new legal case first reported by the Financial Times.

The legislation compels companies to provide information to law enforcement agencies working on cases including terrorism and child sexual abuse. This can include forcing companies to provide the UK security services with access to customer data, even if such information is protected by secure encryption.

The court sent an order giving notice of the new Apple complaint to the human rights group Privacy International, which, alongside fellow campaigner Liberty, had previously launched a separate complaint against TCNs at the IPT.

Among the submissions made by the campaigners were requests for Apple’s claims to be held in public given the public interest in the matter, and a complaint “disputing the lawfulness, necessity and secrecy of the purported Apple TCN and the legal regime underpinning TCNs in general”.

A case management hearing to discuss how the parallel complaints should be handled had been scheduled for next month, Privacy International said.

A spokesperson added: “We are happy to learn that Apple is once again challenging the UK’s regime of secret orders. While we don’t know the substance of Apple’s claim, if it relates to the previously reported orders aimed at undermining the security of Apple’s iCloud storage, then Apple’s claim, alongside ours and Liberty’s, is crucially important to preserving all of our privacy and security.”

Neither Apple nor the Home Office responded to requests for comment. Both are legally restricted from discussing TCNs.

The original TCN issued last year asked Apple for the right to see users’ encrypted data protected by its advanced data protection (ADP) programme in the event of a national security risk.

Apple said the removal of the tool – which not even it can access – would make users more vulnerable to data breaches from bad actors and other threats to customer privacy. Creating a “back door” would also mean all data was accessible by Apple, which it could be forced to share with law enforcement possessing a warrant.

As a result, Apple withdrew UK customers’ access to its ADP programme in January 2025.

The Home Office has maintained that the Investigatory Powers Act, under which such orders are issued, contains robust safeguards and is used only when absolutely necessary.

title: A Common Thread
description: How the 1/4″-20 UNC camera mount and its anti-twist locating pins became the mechanical interface for projects around my apartment.
fullText:
Around the middle of 2019, I started making the equipment around me speak one
electrical language. I built a USB Power Delivery sink controller, then
converted more and more of my
equipment to USB-C. The point was not the connector itself. It was being
able to reach for one cable and one power supply with some confidence that
things would work together.

Quite by accident, I have done the same thing mechanically. The interface is
the ordinary camera tripod thread: 1/4″-20 UNC. Once I noticed the absurd
range of clamps, ball heads, quick-release plates and articulating arms built
around it, I stopped treating them as camera equipment. They are a mature box
of mechanical parts that happen to have escaped from photography.

The smaller camera thread has a nominal 1/4-inch diameter and 20 threads per
inch in the Unified National Coarse series. Together with the larger 3/8″-16
thread, it is specified by ISO 1222 for connecting cameras, tripods and accessories.
The interesting part is everything that followed: decades of compatible gear
designed to hold a load, put it at a useful angle and stay there.

That ecosystem is far more useful to me than another bespoke bracket. A new
project only needs to expose the thread. I can then choose an existing arm,
clamp or plate, change it later, or borrow a part from another setup without
redesigning the object.

Converting an existing object is wonderfully uneventful. In material thick
enough to hold a useful thread, I drill the appropriate tapping-size hole and
run a 1/4″-20 UNC tap through it. Drilling makes the hole; tapping is
the term for cutting the internal thread. In thin or brittle material, a
threaded insert or a through-bolt is the honest solution instead.

The luckiest conversion was an IKEA STÄNKREGN LED ring lamp (005.421.54).
Its proprietary pivot hole was already exactly the right size. I removed the
original stand and screwed a camera mount into the plastic, cutting the thread
as it went. It looks as if it was designed for the little tripod, although
neither manufacturer had the other in mind.

The plain thread has one irritating weakness: it is also an axis. An
off-centre load applies torque around the screw, so a heavy light or long arm
has to be tightened hard enough for friction alone to stop it rotating. That
works, until it doesn’t.

Then I found the refinement I had been missing: a 1/4″-20 locating screw with
two retractable anti-twist pins, commonly described as ARRI locating pins.
The SmallRig arm I use calls them exactly that.
On a plain surface the pins retract and the ordinary screw still works. Give
them two matching holes, however, and the screw supplies the clamping force
while the pins take the torque.

Once I understood the arrangement, I added the two locating holes to the
mounts I had already made. This is a particularly nice extension: old and new
parts remain compatible, but parts that know about the extra holes get a much
stronger connection.

The camera catalogue now supplies the joints for my lights. A compact panel
can sit beside or above the laptop, then move out of the way with one lever.

The same parts scale to a much larger LED panel. The light, arm and cabinet
clamp remain separate, replaceable objects; the thread is the only agreement
between them.

I love a simple design that remains useful far beyond anything its makers
could have predicted. That is not luck. Luck was the hole in the IKEA light.
Foresight is putting just enough constraint into an interface that
people can adapt it with confidence, while leaving paths open for uses and
improvements that do not exist yet.

The camera industry did not need to foresee my cup holder, laptop platform or
apartment lighting. It only had to hold a diameter, a thread pitch and a mating
surface steady for long enough that an ecosystem could compound around them.
Later, two optional holes improved the connection without invalidating the
original one. That is excellent design: decide what must stay fixed, and leave
the rest of the future alone.

USB-C gave my equipment a common electrical language. The 1/4″-20 thread has
quietly become the mechanical one.

title: Apple challenges the UK's second attempt to gain access to iCloud data
description: Apple is back in a UK court over government demands for access to encrypted iCloud data, months after it degraded security for British users rather than build the back door the UK wanted.
fullText:
Apple has launched a fresh legal challenge against the UK government's demand for access to its customers' encrypted data, months after it withdrew a security feature for UK users rather than comply with an earlier version of the same request.

The US technology company filed a complaint last month with the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT), an independent court that examines claims of unlawful conduct by UK intelligence services.

At the heart of the dispute is whether the UK government can force Apple to give it access to iCloud data that is otherwise protected by encryption so strong that even Apple cannot read it.

According to an order issued by the court, the Home Office made a second request for backdoor access to encrypted iCloud data belonging to British users.

The UK backed down on its original demand last year after a heated dispute with Washington. That first order, issued under the Investigatory Powers Act in January 2025, sought access to UK and US customers' data alike.

Authorities subsequently narrowed their approach, issuing a new "technical capability notice" (TCN) limited to UK users only later in 2025, which is the order Apple is now contesting.

TCNs compel companies to hand law enforcement agencies information for cases including terrorism and child sexual abuse, even where that data is protected by encryption.

Apple has long insisted it will not build any form of compelled access into its products.

The company has argued more broadly that any such tool, once built, poses a security risk to all users, not just those targeted by a specific request.

It withdrew UK customers' access to Advanced Data Protection, an optional iCloud security feature that encrypts data so thoroughly that even Apple cannot read it, after receiving the original order in February 2025.

Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in feature that adds end-to-end encryption on top of iCloud's standard encryption, covering things like device backups, photos and notes.

Apple can restrict who is offered it by account region and country settings, the same way it restricts other region-specific features.

Technical capability notices remain shrouded in secrecy by law: companies that receive one cannot confirm its existence, and the government routinely declines to comment on individual cases, citing national security.

That secrecy is itself central to the objections raised by campaign groups, who argue that surveillance powers of this scale should face more public scrutiny than the current legal framework allows.

title: Meat: Use a model to reduce a diff to the important parts
description: meat.dev. Contribute to boldsoftware/meat development by creating an account on GitHub.
fullText:
Abridge a code diff into a reading diff.

Humans need to review agent-written code in critical systems.
But models are good now. You don't need to review for style or nil-checks
or imports. You need to review concepts, algorithm choices, architecture.

So meat uses a model to reduce a diff to the important parts.
It shows you the meat.

Run with meat to review the latest commit.
It takes git-looking parameters to pick commits to review.

It takes a while to process a commit for reading.
So I suggest you have an agent build meat into your devtools so that
it pre-processes it.

Very large diffs are split at file and hunk boundaries and abridged
chunk by chunk (up to a few MB), so one huge commit still produces a
single merged reading diff — it just takes proportionally longer.

description: Economics editor Faisal Islam examines whether the north-west city can be a template for the entire country.
fullText:
It was just five months ago when Andy Burnham retreated to his mayor's office in Manchester, having been blocked by Labour's ruling executive from standing for parliament.

When I met him there a few weeks later, he told me he planned to deal with his disappointment with some ambitious plans for his city region.

Burnham told me he wanted to appeal directly to Fifa to host the final of the women's football World Cup in 2035 Manchester instead of Wembley. "Imagine how electrifying that is for any girl growing up in the north of England," he said.

He said he was also joining forces with other mayors for a "Great Northern" Olympic bid across the north of England, and a plan was also afoot to host the Ryder Cup in Bolton. Sports bodies needed "re-educating" about the rest of the country, he said.

Manchester has already poached the Brit Awards from London after half a century in the capital.

Big, bold gestures like these tell part of the story of what has happened in the city. Burnham's civic ambition is a byproduct of Manchester's status as the fastest-growing city economy in the country. As Burnham prepares to become prime minister, will he be able to apply the same model to the whole of the nation?

Even before Burnham returned to parliament in June, there has been talk of Manchesterism as a political-economic philosophy that offers a programme for national transformation, rooted in a critique of a currently unresponsive, over-centralised British state.

The city has a long history of blending the freest of free markets with a strong social spirit. Manchester's cotton traders championed free trade and liberal economics, at the same time as the emergence of the co-operative movement, the trade unions and the Suffragettes. Even the Manchester Ship Canal, the emblem of monopoly-breaking free trade, required local government intervention backed by the workers.

But for an understanding of contemporary Manchester, you need to go back to the summer of 1996.

Andy Burnham had left the north-west of England by then. He told me how when he first looked for a local media job after graduating in the early 1990s, all he could get was a role as an unpaid reporter on the Middleton Guardian.

"I had to do what so many people of my generation, born in the 60s or 70s in the north-west of England had to do to get on in life," he said. "We had to go south."

The reconstruction in the aftermath of the attack marked the start of Manchester's ascent from the doldrums of de-industrialisation. The essential idea provided by a group of local political, cultural and business leaders, and an architect called Ian Simpson, was that the city centre should be reshaped by demolishing, not repairing, many of the damaged buildings.

From disaster could then arise a great opportunity to reshape the city's geography and economy. Council leader Sir Richard Leese and his top civil servant, the late Sir Howard Bernstein set the tone for a variety of bold centrally driven strategic plans that were actually largely delivered by private capital and then significant international investment.

The council leadership was ruthlessly focused on transforming brownfield industrial sites. The private sector would go nowhere near them, but the council de-risked those investments with public money. It also sometimes stepped in to tide projects over during financial crises.

At the end of this process, private capital poured in, lining up the cranes and the hard hats. The council offered a flexible interpretation of requirements to build a proportion of "affordable housing", sometimes effectively waived, sometimes met by funding building in cheaper areas of the city.

Paul Thwaite, the chief executive of NatWest, which has funded some of these projects, and who is on the board of the University of Manchester, says Manchester's success story over the past 20 years was "built on there being a clear plan the private sector can get behind".

Such a shift would have been unthinkable a generation ago. The model of Manchester's city centre development has succeeded in creating a critical mass of population, housing, jobs and service sector activity that has allowed it to turn its significant undergraduate population into a goldmine.

According to the mayor, more people from London had moved to Manchester (13,000) than the other way round (11,800) in the latest set of internal migration figures.

He put this down to a flow of young workers into the Manchester city centre service economy.

In a reverse from the 1990s, "no-one here has to leave to get on in life", Burnham told me. "And in fact, there's a net inflow of young people from London."

Manchester now retains over half its graduates, more than any other city apart from London, according to the Centre for Cities, and Manchester also attracts almost as many young graduates as it produces.

Tom Beahon, the CEO of Manchester-based sports brand Castore, who has not been shy about criticising some of the government's business policies, told our Big Boss podcast earlier this year that the mayor had helped "attract inbound investment, making it a place that students want to stay after they graduate from the fantastic universities". That in turn means more businesses want to launch in the city, he added.

It is a case study in agglomeration effects - the economic power of locating similar types of jobs close together. And if its infrastructure can keep up, Manchester's economy will continue to fly.

Andy Burnham is a product of this Greater Manchester and spent his decade as its first mayor trying to shape it. As Andy Spinoza, the foremost chronicler of Manchester's turnaround, puts it: "Burnham jumped into a moving car, and by the end he was driving it."

But what else is there to Burnham beyond driving that moving car?

While he has managed to ascend to the Labour leadership and the cusp of No 10 without revealing his wider policy plans, there is a fairly recent text already out there. In 2024 with his fellow north-west regional mayor, Merseyside's Steve Rotherham, he published a book called Head North: A Rallying Cry for a More Equal Britain.

It was the basis for Burnham's speech earlier this month on Manchesterism and remains his national political-economic-constitutional prospectus. The 10-point plan to "rewire" the country argues that better "homes, transport and jobs" across the country can only come from "a new set of principles and rules for the running of the British state".

What underpins this is a determination to tear up two formulas that have long formed the backbone of how UK governments allocate money. The first is the Treasury's Green Book, which decides infrastructure spending and which has traditionally valued existing areas of high growth and land value the most. In Burnham's view, this drags investment in transport to the south of England.

The tangible example of all of this can be found on Platforms 13 and 14 of Piccadilly station in central Manchester. The only east-west train link for both the city centre and the North's main international airport is here, and it is often jam-packed with trains and 40,000 daily passengers attempting to cross the Pennines, or get to the airport, or to Merseyside. Burnham has long advocated for an underground four-platform "Kings Cross of the North" with a northern version of London's Elizabeth Line.

He relays a story about his time as chief secretary to the Treasury in 2007 when he was told: "No project in the north passed the Green Book, Minister." He told me the same in 2020 when there were murmurings of reform to the formula. Chancellor Rachel Reeves pursued pilot projects to change the approach that could favour local investment.

In the book, Burnham also advocates tearing up the Barnett formula, which allocates public spending, topping up spend for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland so they do not lose out to England as a whole. The effect, Burnham argues, is that the north of England is left squeezed in a "pincer".

In Head North and his recent speech, Burnham points to Germany's "Basic Law", with its duty of "equivalent living standards" across the regions. Such a law, he argued, would protect local government and give regions a right to be consulted on long-term decisions.

Burnham also advocates significant constitutional change, including a form of proportional representation and the replacement of the House of Lords with a "Senate of the Nations and the Regions", alongside devolution of powers over large swathes of public services to regional level.

On Net Zero he proposes a "Northern Way", which subsidises the transition, retrofits, cutting bills, and building exportable locally owned industry. He contrasts this with a "Whitehall way", which he characterises as bans, charges and taxes that hit the poorest.

The actual policy consequence of this will have to reckon with rising global energy prices, pressure on household budgets, and some impatience from North Sea energy interests to pump more oil and gas. There are some contradictions in for example, full tax and spend devolution for every region. Would the south-east get to keep the taxes it raises? Some aides recently played down any changes to the Barnett formula amid concerns from Scottish politicians.

The fundamental difference between running a city region and a country is the need to raise the entire spectrum of tax revenues to fund spending. Or to borrow more money. The picture is rather constrained on both right now. Manchester has been agile in attracting private capital to build infrastructure, especially housing, partly because it had to. Can that stretch across the whole country?

With Manchester's cotton traders in mind, I asked Burnham back in February if he considered the Manchester model to be politically left or right - an example of statism, perhaps?

"When it comes to right versus left, well, we've always been very pro-business, pro-enterprise here. We want people to succeed individually and businesses to succeed, but give back at the same time," he said.

Some campaigners say that the dash for the gleaming towers and spires in the centre has left behind much of the rest of the region, and that the centre of Manchester is becoming a mini-London. While Burnham has criticised decades of "neoliberalism" and the "trickle-down effect", the reality is it has been core to the Manchester model.

At the same time, Margaret Thatcher's 1985 bus deregulation has been reversed and over the years public money from central and local government, from the EU, as well as from the partly council-owned airport, has been spent on trams - a nod to the importance of spreading the proceeds of growth in the centre around the region.

To greater or lesser degrees Burnham has floated more "public control", cost of living support, small business rates relief, and higher infrastructure investment and higher defence spending. They sound difficult to reconcile with sticking to promises to limit borrowing and not raise major taxes.

For example, the Defence Investment Plan is "funded" by cuts to capital investment in transport, energy and elsewhere. These are precisely the areas that Manchesterism would suggest might get more central capital investment.

Burnham the mayor has beaten the drum for the new Liverpool-Manchester Northern Powerhouse Rail and the high speed Manchester-Birmingham line he worked up with former West Midlands Mayor Andy Street. But what will Prime Minister Burnham do?

After record heat, could the Atlantic make Britain's weather even more extreme?

We are living fewer years in good health: Is the NHS part of the problem?

The youth clubs fighting to stay relevant in the social media age

And what about the paused Brexit reset? There was a deal ready to go for closer relations at a UK-EU summit originally planned for next week. The government had started to explore different red lines for the next Labour manifesto and a turn back towards Europe's single market. Does he go with Remainy Manchester? Or do the feelings of his Leave constituency, Makerfield, trump all?

NatWest's Paul Thwaite says there could be a "powerful recipe for sustained growth" from the private capital that flows from "long-term certainty and genuine collaboration". There isn't, however, a "single blueprint" from Manchester or anywhere, he says. For devolution to work "the institutions, the leadership and the commercial capability matter as much as the powers themselves".

Burnham in his speech quoted the famous line attributed to Tony Wilson in the film 24 Hour Party People: "It's Manchester, we do things differently here." Now it's time to reveal what exactly it means for the nation.

Clarification 31 July: We have amended a passage in this article to make clear that Manchester Piccadilly station is Greater Manchester's only link for trains going from east to west across the Pennines, and that Platforms 13 and 14 are for services to the east coast, to Merseyside and the city's airport.
