title: Idaho In-N-Out shooting: Good Samaritan who confronted gunman speaks out
description: The private citizen recounts confronting the gunman during the deadly shooting.
fullText:
A private citizen who confronted the gunman who killed three people and wounded seven others outside an In-N-Out Burger in Twin Falls, Idaho, is speaking out about his encounter with the shooter.

Jordan Salinas, 35, told ABC News he spotted the suspect aiming a rifle at passing vehicles before confronting him.

"I peeked around the right-hand side of that sign closest to the road, and that's when I saw the individual with his rifle pointed at the vehicles," Salinas said.

Salinas said the suspect appeared calm as he aimed at cars but that his demeanor changed once shots were fired in his direction.

"He seemed unusually comfortable aiming that rifle at those cars," Salinas said. "As soon as some rounds started coming at him, everything changed immediately. All that bravado he had immediately crumbled."

According to Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks, Salinas and an armed off-duty Idaho State Police trooper confronted the suspect, 24-year-old Chad Williams, who later died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

"We believe these actions drove the suspect from the scene and prevented further casualties," Hicks said during a Sunday news conference.

Authorities said three people were killed and seven others were injured in the shooting Saturday afternoon outside the In-N-Out Burger on Blue Lakes Boulevard. Five of the injured victims remained hospitalized Sunday, including two in critical condition, according to Hicks.

3 killed, 7 injured in shooting at In-N-Out in Idaho, police say

Investigators believe Williams acted alone, and a motive remains under investigation. Police said his family is cooperating with investigators.

Lynsi Snyder, president of In-N-Out Burger, said in a statement posted to social media that one of the company's employees was among those killed.

"In-N-Out will be mourning with the families and praying for them as they tread through a very painful season," Snyder said.

Off-duty officer and citizen confronted shooter at In-N-Out in Idaho, officials say

Police responded to reports of gunfire at about 2:29 p.m. Saturday. Hicks said 911 dispatchers could hear screams and gunfire in the background of emergency calls.

He described the scene as "one of the most chaotic instances a law enforcement officer could face in their career," noting the restaurant is located near a busy shopping area where potentially hundreds of people were nearby at the time of the shooting.

The FBI is assisting the investigation, and authorities continue to ask anyone with information or video of the shooting to come forward.

ABC News' Tonya Kerr and John Capell contributed to this report.

title: Former Ukrainian top commander sees no prospect of Kyiv joining NATO
description: (Corrects paragraph 8 to say Zaluzhnyi was dismissed as Ukraine's top commander in 2024, not last year) Aug 3 () - Ukraine's former ‌top military commander, now ambassador to Britain, was quoted as ‌s...
fullText:
(Corrects paragraph 8 to say Zaluzhnyi was dismissed as Ukraine's top commander in 2024, not last year)

Aug 3 (Reuters) - Ukraine's former ‌top military commander, now ambassador to Britain, was quoted as ‌saying on Monday that there was no prospect of the country joining NATO, an ​aspiration entrenched in the constitution.

Valery Zaluzhnyi, quoted by media outlet Evropeiska Pravda, told a meeting of Ukrainian ambassadors that Ukraine in no way met the military standards needed to join the alliance.

"I know NATO really well. For ‌about 12 years, I personally ⁠worked on making sure we met NATO standards, and every year I heard tales about how we would ⁠join NATO any day now," Evropeiska Pravda quoted him as telling the meeting.

"Unfortunately, we will never actually join."

Zaluzhnyi said it was "impossible with the level of ​development that ​the Armed Forces of Ukraine have … ​to join an organisation guided ‌by World War II doctrines".

Ukraine needed the technology "already in use in NATO member-states, including anti-missile defence, space capabilities etc", he was quoted as saying.

Ukraine has enshrined in its constitution a strategic goal of membership of NATO and the European Union. It has, however, acknowledged that currently it would ‌not be welcomed into NATO by all ​its members.

Zaluzhnyi was dismissed as Ukraine's top ​commander in 2024 over differences ​with President Volodymyr Zelenskiy on conducting the war with ‌Russia, now well into its fifth ​year.

Opinion surveys on ​voter trust put him roughly on a par with Zelenskiy and with former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, sacked as defence minister last ​month. Zaluzhnyi's successor ‌as top commander was also dismissed last month.

Russia has rejected out ​of hand any notion of Ukrainian membership of NATO.

title: Man arrested over death of nine-year-old girl found injured in industrial estate
description: The girl, from West Yorkshire, was found injured at the Elliot Industrial Estate in Arbroath shortly after midnight.
fullText:
A man has been arrested after the death of a nine-year-old girl who was found with serious injuries in Arbroath.

Officers were called to the town's Elliot Industrial Estate shortly after midnight.

The girl, from West Yorkshire, was taken to Ninewells Hospital in Dundee, where she later died.

A 35-year-old white British man, who police say was known to the child, has been arrested in connection with her death, which is being treated as suspicious.

Police Scotland said officers were not looking for anyone else in connection with her death.

It said the other members of the family, who were camping in the area, are being supported by specialist officers.

It is understood that no one else was injured.

A police forensics tent has been erected at the scene and a cordon has been put in place.

Police Scotland said the girl's family were being supported by specialist officers and inquiries were continuing.

Karen Youngson said she had picked up her friend from the gym on the estate at about 22:15 on Sunday and had seen a small tent and some camping chairs.

She said: "When I first went up there, I was like my goodness why is there a tent there?

"There were two camping chairs, that's all I saw, but it was the amount of rubbish, it was unbelievable."

When she returned from collecting her friend, she said they had to slow down to avoid a baby seagull on the road.

She said: "It was dark, there was no noise coming from the place, it wasn't like there were lights or anyone sitting outside."

A man who works on the industrial estate, who did not want to be named, said he had seen a small tent with a car parked beside it at about 18:15 on Sunday.

He said he had seen a man and woman and two children there, either making or clearing up food.

The man said that when he passed the tent about 30 minutes later, the people were still there.

He said: "I thought it was a pretty strange place to camp, especially given the beach at Elliot which is two minutes away and is obviously a bit more picturesque."

Arbroath East and Lunan councillor Lois Speed said it was a "heartbreaking morning."

She said: "I think everybody is just feeling at a loss for words, because it is just devastating.

"I have not spoken to anyone directly but (from) the social media shares and comments, everyone is just shocked and saddened.

"I think everyone's thoughts are with those directly impacted, the wee girl, her family and everyone close.

"Everyone will be thinking of them and how difficult this must be."

title: Supreme Court won't halt $656M judgment against the PLO and Palestinian Authority
description: Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor refused Monday to halt a $656 million judgment against Palestinian authorities in a long-running lawsuit filed by Americans killed or wounded in attacks in Israel...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor refused Monday to halt a $656 million judgment against Palestinian authorities in a long-running lawsuit filed by Americans killed or wounded in attacks in Israel.

The order signed by Sotomayor comes after the high court ruled last year in favor of the victims and their families.

The Palestine Liberation Organization and the Palestinian Authority said in court documents that paying the hefty judgment now could destabilize government services in the West Bank. They asked the justices to pause payment as they appeal the reinstatement of the verdict.

The lawsuit was filed by victims of attacks in Jerusalem in the early 2000s that killed 33 people and wounded hundreds more. Families brought their lawsuit under the Anti-Terrorism Act, a law aimed at opening U.S. courts to victims of international terror attacks.

A federal court in New York tossed the original verdict on appeal and continued to rule in favor of the Palestine Liberation Organization and the Palestinian Authority as Congress revised the law to allow suits to go forward. The Supreme Court revived two cases in 2025.

The 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals agreed to reinstate the verdict in March. Attorneys for the plaintiffs said at the time that the families were pleased and relieved by the decision, saying it would allow "justice to be done" after a long legal process.

title: Top Trump ally warns super PAC bankrolled by Dem billionaire is meddling in his GOP primary
description: Rep. Andy Ogles says the $2 million clean energy PAC spending against him in Tennessee's Republican primary proves how much groups profit from subsidies.
fullText:
A clean energy super PAC bankrolled by a left-wing billionaire is pouring millions into an effort to unseat Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., as he wages a bid for re-election in Tennessee's 5th Congressional District.

The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition super PAC had spent roughly $1.3 million on opposing Ogles and supporting his Republican challenger, Charlie Hatcher, Tennessee's former commissioner of agriculture, and recently bought another $700,000 worth of ads.

The group has raised $6.7 million this year, making Ogles a sizable portion of their spending this cycle. A Fox News Digital review of FEC filings discovered that the super PAC is bankrolled by Chris Larsen, the California-based billionaire chairman of Ripple, which is described on its website as the "leading financial technology company that offers crypto solutions for businesses."

Larsen has donated $6 million to the super PAC since Feb. 2026. His latest $5 million donation to Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC is his second-largest single donation after donating $5,444,975 to Future Forward PAC in 2024 to support Kamala Harris's failed presidential campaign.

Trump-backed Firebrand Wins Arizona Gop Governor Primary, Setting Up High-stakes Showdown

Larsen has also donated over $1 million to the Jane Fonda Climate PAC, over $1 million between the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) and Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) and over $300,000 supporting Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., among other six-figure donations to top Democratic campaigns and PACs.

The way that Ogles sees it, it's an attempt to show Republicans what happens when lawmakers attempt to scale back government investments in renewable energy sources.

"When you have a group spending roughly $2 million in a Republican primary, that tells you how much money they're making off of government subsidies, and they're upset that the government welfare has been taken away from them," Ogles told Fox News Digital in an interview.

Larsen, who is an angel investor and climate philanthropist, is making "climate change his top priority," according to an online bio.

"He founded the Larsen Lam Climate Change Foundation (since renamed as the Clean Break Fund) in 2021 to guide his climate philanthropy, and is an active early investor in numerous climate tech companies, as well as several prominent climate funds," the bio continues. "His philanthropic priorities include the climate-driven home insurance crisis, making climate change a bipartisan issue once again, and carbon dioxide removal, among many other projects."

Ogles, a member of the fiscally minded House Freedom Caucus, has been one of the most outspoken Republicans calling for a reversal of energy initiatives passed under President Joe Biden. Among them, Ogles has argued against clean energy subsidies in Biden's Infrastructure and Jobs Act and the Inflation Reduction Act.

But more than that, Ogles thinks it's his proximity to Trump that has made him a target.

"It's because I'm close to the president. It is because I am outspoken. And quite frankly, it is because I speak plainly on these issues," Ogles said.

Trump, who has endorsed Ogles, reaffirmed his support for the conservative firebrand ahead of the primary.

"Andy will be really enshrined as one of the best congressmen that you'll ever see. He's just fantastic," Trump said. "Andy has always been there when we needed him and when I needed him. He's been a great help. He's been a source of inspiration to a lot of people in Congress."

Figures who have donated to Invest in Tomorrow framed energy policy as an issue with electoral consequences, hinting that Ogles is on the wrong side of the issue.

Trump's Ambitious Energy Bet Could Be A Winning Hand As The World Burns More Oil, Gas Than Ever

"Our campaign is here to show that politicians who oppose clean energy do so at their own political peril. Andy Ogles is next," Tom Matzzie, the PAC's executive chairman, said in a statement to Axios.

Matzzie is also CEO of a solar energy company, CleanChoice Energy.

When asked about the comment, Ogles said he doesn't think his views are at odds with the way voters see energy and has characterized the opposition spending as an attempt to buy a seat energy groups can control.

"If trying to build an energy sector that is self-reliant, because it's a national security issue, makes me an extremist, then so be it."

Ogles said he stands by his all-of-the-above energy stance. In his view, it's not the government's job to pick winners and losers in the energy market — especially in light of the country's overspending challenges.

"I'm not against solar. We have a farm. I've got a big shop. You know, I've contemplated putting solar on my shop to help to run my farm. But I don't want a government subsidy to make it work. I don't need a government subsidy to pay for it," Ogles said.

Dem Supported 'Green New Deal' After Receiving Nearly $60K From Energy Groups, Now Wants Congressional Seat

"Look, at the end of the day, you know, I voted for conservative policies and that's what America wants right now. We're barreling towards $40 trillion in debt," he added.

The Tennessee primary will take place on Thursday, Aug. 6.

title: Ethics panel recommends House censure Rep. Chuck Edwards for conduct with two aides
description: The House Ethics Committee recommended Monday that Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., be censured after finding that he engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct toward two young female ...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The House Ethics Committee recommended Monday that Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., be censured after finding that he engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct toward two young female aides in his congressional office.

A censure registers the House's deep disapproval of a lawmaker's conduct that does not meet the threshold for expulsion.

Edwards, 65, has denied that any of his conduct was intended as a sexual or romantic advance, but the committee said his behavior would "lead a reasonable observer to interpret it as such." It also described his actions as "beyond inappropriate."

The panel highlighted numerous examples of actions it considered improper, including Edwards providing the young women with lavish and recurrent gifts, making comments regarding their appearance and dress, inviting them to intimate dinners and vacations, and sending notes regarding his affection.

The Ethics panel found no evidence Edwards explicitly propositioned any person under his employ or engaged in any sexual activity with them. But it also said he failed to adhere to "the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers."

"Both women were uncomfortable with his behavior (which they attempted to communicate) but were put in an untenable position by virtue of his status as their boss and a Member of Congress," the Ethics Committee said in its 25-page report. "Representative Edwards was at minimum blind to that reality, and at worst, dismissive of the impact his inappropriate conduct had on the careers and well-being of two women on his staff."

One aide worked for the congressman's office for about two-and-a-half years and the other for about three years. They no longer work there. The Ethics panel said they left due to conduct described in its report, although they provided other explanations to Edwards.

In a 15-page response to the report, Edwards' attorneys argued that the committee's findings "exonerate" the congressman, pointing to the conclusion that he did not engage in sexual activity or explicitly proposition any staff member.

His attorneys said the recommendation of censure was an "extraordinarily harsh and infrequent punishment" that is based on vague standards and adherence to the spirit of House rules, "not based on a direct violation of House rules addressing sexual misconduct."

Paul Shumaker, a spokesperson and strategist for Edwards' reelection campaign, said the Ethics Committee's staff took it upon themselves to write rules inconsistent with the written rule of law or House rules.

"Representative Edwards looks forward to having his name cleared and will work to ensure that the full light of day is brought on this process and that every member of Congress and the public can see the attempt to harm the Congressman who has brought no harm to others," Shumaker said in a written statement.

The committee's report detailed numerous gifts that Edwards gave the two aides, calling the gifts "beyond norms of professional behavior." The women received jewelry totaling more than $1,000, designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, as well as vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners.

House members are prohibited from engaging in sexual harassment or making unwanted advances toward their subordinates.

The Edwards investigation came at a time of heightened scrutiny of lawmakers' behavior toward female staffers following the resignations of Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell and Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales. Both were facing calls for their expulsion before they stepped down earlier this year.

In May, House leadership designated Reps. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., and Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., to lead a bipartisan effort to combat sexual misconduct in Congress. Their work is focused on making Capitol Hill a safer job environment for women.

The Ethics panel said Edwards cooperated with the investigation and acknowledged to them that at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate. However, he has not acknowledged or taken responsibility for the harm he caused, the committee said.

In his interview with the committee, the panel said Edwards repeatedly asserted that he knows well what constitutes "sexual harassment," and seemed to believe he had immunized himself from such a charge by avoiding inappropriate touching and sexual comments and occasionally telling the staffers that they were free to put up boundaries.

"Despite the absence of an explicit proposition, a reasonable person could interpret Representative Edwards' intimate and effusive attentions, where he prioritized the personal over the professional, as thinly veiled advances," the committee wrote.

The full House will have to vote before any censure would occur. Traditionally, a lawmaker who is censured must stand in the well of the House while the speaker or presiding officer reads the censure resolution as a form of public rebuke.

Lawmakers are back in their home districts for almost the rest of the month, so a vote on whether to censure Edwards won't occur for a few weeks at the earliest.

title: Three officers injured after eggs and bricks thrown at police
description: Police were called to reports of a group protesting outside a house on Priesthill Road about 18:55 on Sunday.
fullText:
An investigation is underway after officers were injured when eggs and bricks were thrown at them by a crowd gathered outside a house in Glasgow.

Police were called to reports of a group protesting outside a house on Priesthill Road at around 18:55 on Sunday. Officers attended and removed the occupants of the house.

The crowd, some with their faces covered, refused to disperse and became hostile to officers.

Three officers were injured and three police vehicles were damaged, resulting in one being taken out of service.

Local Area Commander, Ch Insp William Campbell said: "The disorder seen last night is unacceptable, and I would like to reassure the local community that our investigation is continuing to identify those responsible and take the appropriate action.

"I am aware of online misinformation being circulated last night and I would urge the public to behave responsibly around social media, particularly with information being shared and the response to what is read or seen online."

He said they are reviewing videos of the incident to identify those responsible and asked for anyone with footage to contact Police Scotland.

title: Contractors building border wall ordered to stop drilling wells in drought-stricken New Mexico
description: The Trump administration has ordered construction crews on a border wall to stop drilling wells in drought-stricken New Mexico after ranchers said pumping groundwater needed to make concrete could thr...
fullText:
PHOENIX (AP) — The Trump administration has ordered construction crews on a border wall to stop drilling wells in drought-stricken New Mexico after ranchers said pumping groundwater needed to make concrete could threaten their livestock.

The order comes as crews across the southern border race to complete one of President Donald Trump's highest domestic priorities — barriers that span four states and received over $46 billion in federal funding. Controversies have sprouted up in Texas and California, with border-town residents and environmentalists reporting a wide variety of issues with construction.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection, which oversees border wall construction, has said water is needed to make concrete for roads, wall construction and dust suppression. Cattle ranchers in the area say the drought has already forced them to reduce their herd size.

"It would put us in an immediate catastrophe and having to do something with our livestock. I mean, it could potentially put some people out of business, us included," said Russell Johnson, a cattle rancher whose property runs along the border.

Johnson raised the issue at a public meeting in July after noticing an industrial well, which drilling crews told him would pump 300 gallons a minute, on land he leases for grazing. Johnson has roughly 12 wells across his ranch, which pump between three and seven gallons a minute.

A spokesperson for CBP said on Monday that border wall contractors in New Mexico have been instructed to stop drilling new wells, but did not comment on whether the wells already drilled could be pumped. The agency said they would collaborate with New Mexico and the U.S. Department of Agriculture to develop a groundwater strategy.

"CBP is committed to working collaboratively with local landowners to ensure that construction activities do not adversely impact their water needs," read the statement.

The federal contractors building the wall in New Mexico — Caddell Construction Co. and Fisher Industries — did not respond to emails or phone calls seeking comment. Messages left with receptionists for Barnard Construction and Spencer Construction Co., the contractors building near Johnson's ranch, were not immediately returned.

The New Mexico Office of the State Engineer, which monitors and approves wells across the state, said staff have counted eight wells drilled without the office's permission along the southern border, but cautioned there could be more. Staff visited two wells in July and reported they were pumping 200 gallons per minute.

"All non-tribal wells in New Mexico, whether they are drilled on state or federal land, must have permits from the state engineer before they can be drilled or water can be pumped from them," the Office of the State Engineer said in a statement.

The wells for border construction were all drilled on a federally owned strip of land 60 miles (96 kilometers) north of the border called the Roosevelt Reservation. CBP did not respond to follow up questions about whether the federal government has a right to pump groundwater on federal land without state oversight.

Tom Patterson, president of the New Mexico Cattle Growers' Association, says water is the No. 1 concern for ranchers and that if wells start to go dry, it's already too late. During wall construction in Trump's first term, Patterson said, contractors bought water from farms, ranches, or municipalities in the area, which meant the amount of water being pumped from nearby basins didn't increase during construction.

"Why do they need all this water?" said Patterson. "And why can't they buy it as they have in the past from farmers, ranchers, or even from Luna County?"

Johnson said the moratorium on future well drilling is a step in the right direction, but he's still worried after a contractor told him the well near his ranch could eventually be pumped if crews ended up needing the water. Though beef prices are up, Johnson has been forced to reduce his herd to one third its original capacity. He cites the drought, which has left less grass for cattle to graze on, as the main reason for the drop.

Before the first border wall went up, Johnson remembers seeing at least one truck of people crossing his ranch every week. Now, he says illegal crossing hardly ever happens on his ranch. As a former Border Patrol agent, he supports the border wall but doesn't believe it should cost him his livelihood.

So far, half a mile of secondary wall has gone up near Johnson's property.

"They need to stop pumping all of these wells because they were all drilled illegally," Johnson said.

Both candidates in the race for a congressional seat that represents this area in New Mexico claimed credit for the moratorium.

Congressional candidate Greg Cunningham, a Republican, said he advocated for the agreement between CBP and border wall contractors and was the first to announce the news over social media on Friday.

"Ranchers, families and local officials brought us their concerns. I raised it with the Trump Administration. They listened. They acted fast," Cunningham said in a post on X.

Congressman Gabe Vasquez, who faces Cunningham in November's midterm elections, spoke about the issue on the House floor earlier this month.

"This illegal drilling by this administration should never have happened, but when it did, I heard our ranchers' concerns loud and clear and immediately raised hell in Washington to get the job done and protect New Mexicans' water rights."

title: Deadliest animal in every US state revealed, from moose and bears to dogs
description: A new report identifies the deadliest animal in every U.S. state, with snakes leading nationwide while bears, sharks, insects and even dogs top other regions.
fullText:
A demographic data platform has released a new report identifying the animals most likely to kill people in each U.S. state.

The 2026 report from World Population Review revealed a surprising mix of creatures topping the list, from large mammals such as moose to unexpected threats such as dogs and jellyfish.

According to the report, snakes make up the single largest category nationwide, with several species of rattlesnakes topping the list in multiple regions.

Georgia residents should be most cautious of the pygmy rattlesnake, while Oklahoma's biggest snake threat is the western pygmy rattlesnake.

Meanwhile, Timber rattlesnakes claimed the top spot in both Connecticut and Kansas.

Southern Pacific rattlesnakes pose the biggest threat in California, while Arizona's deadliest species is the western diamondback rattlesnake.

Other rattlesnakes dominating state hazards include the prairie rattlesnake in North Dakota, the Mojave rattlesnake in Nevada and the eastern massasauga in Michigan.

Several non-rattlesnake species also rank as the deadliest animals in their respective states.

Louisiana's top threat is the eastern diamondback rattlesnake and Mississippi's is the cottonmouth snake.

Similarly, Indiana leads with the eastern copperhead, South Carolina points to the southern copperhead, and Hawaii stands out with the yellow-bellied sea snake as its primary concern.

No Cure, No Vaccine: Experts Warn Of Rare Bourbon Virus After First Ny Case

Beyond reptiles, several states face risks from insects and other venomous creatures.

Wasps top the list in Iowa, ticks take the lead in Missouri, mosquitoes pose the highest danger in New York, and black widow spiders are the main concern in Alabama and Nebraska.

A handful of states should be cautious around coastal waters, according to the report.

Tiger sharks rank as the deadliest animal in Rhode Island, while bull sharks pose the greatest threat in Maryland and Virginia.

A jellyfish-like marine creature, called the Portuguese man o' war, is listed as the biggest danger in Delaware and North Carolina. Experts say that while its sting can be deadly in rare cases, it more commonly causes painful welts and skin irritation.

Alligators also rank as the deadliest animal in Florida and Texas, with the American alligator specifically topping Florida's list.

Large mammals also appear prominently throughout the report, with black bears ranking as the deadliest animals in Tennessee and Wisconsin.

North American black bears pose the greatest threat in Oregon, while American black bears top the list in Kentucky and Massachusetts.

In contrast, New Mexico's deadliest animal is the mountain lion, while moose are listed as the greatest risk in Colorado, Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont.

Grizzly bears also top the list in Idaho, Montana and Washington, and bison pose the greatest danger in South Dakota and Wyoming.

Whitetail deer were also identified as the deadliest animals in Arkansas, Ohio, West Virginia and Pennsylvania.

In Alaska, despite commonly being household pets, dogs are listed as the state's most concerning animal.

Similarly, coyotes rank as the biggest threat in Illinois, Minnesota, New Jersey and Utah.

Overall, snakes dominate the threat landscape, topping the list in 14 states, according to the report.

Bears threaten eight states, while deer and other large ungulates account for 10 states.

Canines, including dogs and coyotes, rank as the deadliest animals in five states.

Biting and stinging arthropods, such as wasps, mosquitos and spiders, account for five states.

Equally, marine hazards also account for five states.

title: The summer that changed Welsh football
description: A decade on from Euro 2016, key figures tell BBC Sport Wales the inside story of the summer that changed Welsh football forever.
fullText:
"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were."

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

An anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it."

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible."

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

"That was our best performance," says Coleman. "We were awesome."

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on."

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it."

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open – his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley – to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations."

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space."

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu says. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition."

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour."

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," says Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere."

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'."

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really important moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there – and that stems from 2016.

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," says Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

"That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game."

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and said things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football."

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

"Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed."

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 – a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," says Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'."

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening."

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

title: The ex-sandwich maker who cycles to Champions League games
description: Meet Mjallby striker Jacob Bergstrom, a former sandwich maker who cycles to games and hopes to upset Yaya Toure's new club in the Champions League.
fullText:
Jacob Bergstrom never imagined he would be rubbing shoulders with stars like Yaya Toure in the Champions League.

The 31-year-old was never picked up by a youth academy and was still playing amateur football at 22.

Even after joining Mjallby in 2018, he continued working at Subway to make ends meet. He did not become a full-time professional until he was 24.

But over the past year the burly striker has helped Mjallby win the Swedish championship and Swedish Cup for the first time in their 87-year history.

He then scored on his Champions League debut and now aims to help Mjallby continue their fairytale by overcoming Slovan Bratislava, whose new head coach is Champions League winner and former Manchester City midfielder Toure.

"When I first came here, we were in the third division," Bergstrom tells BBC Sport. "I was so happy to sign. It was so big to me then.

"I never dreamed of anything like this. It was like, I didn't even think about it. For me to be here now is crazy, and to do it with Mjallby as well is amazing."

Last season's surprise title triumph made headlines around the world, mainly because of Mjallby's remote location. The club is based in Hallevik, a coastal village in southern Sweden with fewer than 1,000 residents.

As the strongest football team in Blekinge County, Mjallby attract fans from across the region, averaging home crowds of 5,000 last season.

They also attract players such as Bergstrom, who grew up an hour's drive north in Blekinge's capital Karlskrona, a naval city where handball and ice hockey are more popular.

When Bergstrom rejoined Mjallby after a brief spell with Stockholm-based Djurgarden in 2023, he and his wife moved to Hallevik. They and their two children now call it home.

Although Hallevik is a sleepy fishing village come the winter, holidaymakers quadruple its population in the summer.

And Bergstrom likes to cycle to games and training at Mjallby's home ground Strandvallen. It is just 100 metres from the Baltic Sea, nestled between some woods, a campsite and an outdoor swimming pool.

"You have the ocean and the people," adds Bergstrom. "It's so beautiful by the water and the beach.

"In the winter there's not many people here, so it doesn't fit for everyone, but it fits for us."

Mjallby fans now regard Bergstrom as one of them. The 6ft 3in target man has come to embody the underdog mentality of the region's rural communities.

He once celebrated in front of Malmo fans and did not flinch when they showered him with beer, saying later "it tasted very good".

And after last season's win at Mjallby's big-city rivals he grabbed a megaphone and led a chant of "whoever doesn't jump is a Malmo pig".

Despite his and Mjallby's remarkable rise from obscurity, Bergstrom remains a regular guy.

He still cycles to games and fans might still bump into him in the local supermarket, just as BBC Sport did the day after last month's Champions League qualifier at Strandvallen.

There was a carnival atmosphere for Mjallby's first European game against Gibraltar's Lincoln Red Imps. A jazz band welcomed 3,500 fans while another 2,300 carried deckchairs and cool boxes to Hallevik's marina to watch on a big screen.

"[Playing in Europe] is special for the whole village and for everyone here at the club," says Bergstrom.

"Every time I take my bike to the game, I see all the people in their yellow and black shirts. Everyone has flags in their garden. It's so fun to see everyone get together.

"They are so proud to be part of this journey we've made together."

Hallevik has become the second smallest village to stage a Champions League fixture - after Streymnes in the Faroe Islands (population 321).

Before the 3-0 win over the Red Imps, Mjallby fans revealed a tifo which featured a ship and a map of Europe, with a banner which read: "A new chapter in the history books - written by all who dared to dream and those who refused to give up."

Bergstrom said the tifo was unbelievable while captain Jesper Gustavsson had goosebumps. Gustavsson is one of those that refused to give up - literally.

The 31-year-old is the last survivor of the Mjallby team that avoided relegation to the fourth tier - and probable bankruptcy - on the final day of the 2016 season.

"At that time, me and some team-mates were like 'are we gonna quit after this season?'" he says.

"It was tough, but we kept going and now I'm living my dream with Mjallby."

Gustavsson grew up just 20 minutes north of Hallevik. He went to Mjallby games with his dad before making his debut aged 18.

Now the diminutive midfielder leads a loyal, tight-knit group that has a core of local players and punches above its weight.

"It means everything because I've been here my whole life," he says. "Mjallby believed in me so I'm forever grateful."

A 0-0 draw in Gibraltar meant Mjallby progressed to the third qualifying round to meet Slovan Bratislava, who gave Yaya Toure his first managerial job in June.

The ex-Manchester City midfielder helped Barcelona win the 2009 Champions League final at Rome's Stadio Olimpico. Tuesday's first leg at Strandvallen (17:00 BST) will be unlike any Champions League game he's been involved in.

Many away teams do not like visiting Mjallby. They face a long drive through acres of farmland, with virtually nothing of note except Mjallby flags hanging from tractors.

They reach a modest ground with a vociferous home crowd, which is even louder for European games because Mjallby's hardcore fans must relocate to the biggest-seated stand.

Toure, 43, said Mjallby have "something that other teams don't have" and now they face the 24-time Slovakian champions for a place in the Champions League play-offs.

But even if Mjallby don't pull off another upset, they're guaranteed to play in at least this season's Conference League so Bergstrom is set to meet a few more stars yet.

title: Record number of new managers for season like no other
description: The 2026-27 Premier League season has not yet kicked off, but it has already made history for its managerial changes.
fullText:
The 2026-27 Premier League season has not yet kicked off, but it has already made history.

Nine clubs are set to begin the campaign with a new permanent manager - the highest number ever for the top flight's opening weekend.

From Liverpool and Manchester City to Newcastle United and Chelsea, change has swept across almost half the league.

Four pointers to most open Premier League title race in years

The scale of turnover has dramatically reshaped the Premier League's managerial landscape.

Liverpool appointed Andoni Iraola after Arne Slot was sacked, while Manchester City turned to Enzo Maresca following Pep Guardiola's resignation after a trophy-laden spell at Etihad Stadium.

Chelsea turned to Xabi Alonso after Liam Rosenior's ill-fated term came to an end, Bournemouth appointed Marco Rose after Andoni Iraola's contract expired, and Nottingham Forest hired Oliver Glasner following Vitor Pereira's dismissal.

Crystal Palace turned to Pierre Sage after Glasner left at the end of his contract, Fulham appointed Alvaro Arbeloa after Marco Silva's deal expired, while Ipswich Town named Gary O'Neil as successor when Kieran McKenna resigned.

Newcastle United are also expected to appoint Matthias Jaissle after Eddie Howe stepped down, taking the total to nine clubs beginning the season with a new permanent boss.

The previous record came in 2016-17, when eight clubs began the campaign under new management.

That summer included Guardiola's arrival at Manchester City and Antonio Conte's appointment at Chelsea, with the Italian going on to win the title in his first season.

Before that, seven clubs changed manager before the 1995-96 season, while six did so in 2012-13.

Alonso heals Real Madrid scars to lead Chelsea's senior revolution

Top players, title fights - why Iraola feels ready for Liverpool

Arsenal's Mikel Arteta, appointed in December 2019, is now the league's longest-serving manager despite having been in charge for less than seven years.

Only Atletico Madrid's Diego Simeone, who has led the Spanish side since December 2011, has been in charge of a club for longer across Europe's five major leagues.

Closer to home, Aston Villa's Unai Emery and Leeds United's Daniel Farke have been with their current clubs for more than three seasons, while Sunderland boss Regis le Bris, appointed in July 2024, is already the fourth longest-serving manager in the division.

Manchester United boss Michael Carrick illustrates just how quickly things have changed. Although he became the club's permanent manager in May after taking interim charge in January, only 10 Premier League managers have been in post longer than him.

Carrick is also United's seventh permanent manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

Tottenham Hotspur's Roberto de Zerbi, appointed in March, is only one place further back.

New boss Maresca is perfect for Man City - Gvardiol

Another sub-plot this season will be whether the traditional 'new manager bounce' still exists.

The theory suggests teams often enjoy a short-term improvement after appointing a new head coach, helped by renewed motivation, tactical tweaks and a psychological reset.

This season the concept could be tested like never before. Matchweek one is expected to feature three fixtures between clubs led by new managers - Fulham against Chelsea, Manchester City versus Bournemouth, and Liverpool travelling to Newcastle - with each of those teams adapting to new tactical ideas and coaching methods simultaneously.

Liverpool's start is particularly unusual. Iraola's first six Premier League matches will all come against teams under new permanent managers, with Forest, Ipswich, Fulham, Bournemouth and Manchester City following Newcastle.

For the first time since 1985-86, England's top flight will begin without Sir Alex Ferguson, Arsene Wenger, Jose Mourinho, Jurgen Klopp or Guardiola occupying a dugout.

Between them, they have won 26 of the league's 34 titles.

More than that, they defined successive generations of English football. Ferguson's relentless United sides set the standard during the Premier League's formative years before Wenger transformed perceptions of preparation, sports science and nutrition at Arsenal.

Mourinho introduced a new level of tactical pragmatism and psychological warfare, Klopp's high-intensity pressing reshaped Liverpool, and Guardiola's positional football established one of the most dominant teams in English football history.

Only Ferguson, Mourinho and Guardiola have successfully defended a Premier League title, a feat Arteta now has the chance to emulate after leading the Gunners to the championship last season.

His traditional rivals all begin the campaign under new managers, while Carrick starts his first full season as the Red Devils head coach.

Time will tell if the next defining figure emerges immediately. But with the managers who shaped more than three decades of Premier League history now gone, the 2026-27 season marks the beginning of a new chapter.

The upheaval did not begin this summer. The 2025-26 Premier League season featured 11 managerial changes, with Forest among the clubs to make multiple appointments during the campaign.

The average tenure of a top-flight boss now stands at about 20 months, illustrating just how fleeting life in one of football's most demanding jobs can now be.

Recent history also suggests changing manager offers no guarantees. During the 2025-26 season, several clubs that switched coaches continued to struggle. Forest employed three managers during the campaign, Tottenham changed head coach twice, while Chelsea also altered direction before the season ended.

Others, however, did enjoy an immediate uplift. Carrick averaged 2.6 points per game across his first five matches as United boss, while Rosenior collected the same return after taking charge of Chelsea. Rosenior's tenure ultimately proved short-lived, though, with the Blues winning just one of his final eight Premier League matches before he was dismissed.

Research discussed in the Financial Times, external, drawing on findings from Soccernomics by Simon Kuper and Stefan Szymanski, argues that player quality and spending remain stronger predictors of results than managerial changes alone.

Sports consultancy Twenty First Group says coaches often succeed or fail according to the environment they inherit as much as their own abilities.

Since the Premier League began in 1992, only six managers have won the title in their first season in charge of their club.

Mourinho became the first to achieve the feat with Chelsea in 2004-05, before Carlo Ancelotti repeated it with the same club in 2009-10.

Manuel Pellegrini guided Manchester City to the title in his debut campaign in 2013-14, Claudio Ranieri masterminded Leicester City's remarkable triumph in 2015-16, Conte won the league in his first season at Chelsea in 2016-17, and most recently Slot led Liverpool to the championship in his maiden campaign in 2025-26.

With almost half the division beginning the campaign under new leadership, the Premier League enters one of its most unpredictable seasons in recent memory.

title: Why we are still waiting for the 'Newey effect' - F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
fullText:
Formula 1 is now on it summer break before the season resumes with the Dutch Grand Prix, from 21-23 August.

However, BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson is still here to answer your latest questions.

The new Aston Martin package has undoubtedly been a success, but they are still well below expectations. Should we have already seen the 'Newey effect', and if so, why has the designer who is repeatedly described as 'the best' not had the expected impact? - Benjamin

There are logical reasons why the Aston Martin-Honda package - so strong on paper - has not yet come together.

In short, the new 2026 aerodynamic regulations were published on 2 January 2025. But Adrian Newey did not start officially at Aston Martin in his new role as managing technical partner until 2 March.

When he arrived, he asked the team to stop what they had already worked on and switch to his design outline. That put them two months behind already.

Then, the wind tunnel was not ready to receive any modelling until mid-April, so now they were nearly four months behind the others.

On top of that, the team only realised in November last year that Honda was a long way behind on its engine design.

The cumulative effect of all this was seen at the start of the year, when it became obvious the car and the engine were both uncompetitive and unreliable.

In the intervening period, Aston Martin, as Newey put it, "overhauled how we work", improved organisation, put in place different systems, and rethought the car.

The result was the car that made its debut in Hungary, which was significantly lighter and had much improved downforce. It cut lap times by about two seconds, it seems.

The first upgrade of the Honda engine comes at the next race, the Dutch Grand Prix after the summer break, which is expected to reduce some - but by no means all, or even the majority - of the gap to the leading engines.

All of that means it will be 2027 before the first full-fat Newey-led design appears. And its competitiveness will also depend on how Honda gets on with its 2027 engine.

With the sudden arrival of Malaysia on the calendar, how do the drivers, especially those who haven't raced there, prepare for the race? - Jacob

The Malaysian Grand Prix was always renowned as one of the toughest on the calendar, because of the demands placed on the body by the tropical conditions.

But the same goes for Singapore, which was already on the calendar and which is just a week after Malaysia on the latest schedule.

So the drivers will not need to do anything different in their preparations than they would already be doing for Singapore - they often say that the training they do all year is focused on being able to cope with the humidity and heat there.

One problem the introduction of Malaysia does pose, however, is time zones.

For Singapore, the drivers and teams essentially stay on European time, because of the night-race schedule. So, getting up around lunchtime, going to bed around 3-5am.

But Malaysia is a daytime race, so they will have to switch to local time for that one, having been in Azerbaijan the previous weekend, and then migrate back towards European time for Singapore.

However, these are world-class athletes who are used to this sort of thing, so they will be fine.

Five things we've learned from first half of F1 season

If, as looks likely, the F1 season might finish in Europe (probably Italy), will the low temperatures make the race a bit processional with the low temperatures providing low grip? Is there not a better solution available somewhere warmer, South Africa, Portugal or Thailand for instance? - Alan

The end-of-season races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are in doubt because of the ongoing war between the US/Israel and Iran.

If the situation does not improve by the time F1 has to make a decision, which F1 president Stefano Domenicali says is mid-September, then the races will have to be cancelled.

At the moment, the most likely solution is a race in Imola in Italy in early December.

The weather in Italy at that time can be cold, of course. But, as Domenicali pointed out on a call with F1 media last week, perhaps not as cold as in Las Vegas at the end of November.

It gets pretty chilly at night in Las Vegas when the grand prix is on, and the track surface there is especially non-abrasive. And of course, as it's a night race, there is no solar radiation to heat up the track surface, which there would be to some degree in Imola.

So if the tyres can cope with Las Vegas, they can cope with Imola.

Why not somewhere warmer? As ever in F1, the sport does not just put on a race for the sake of there being a race, it also has to make financial and logistical sense.

You say Thailand - there is no track there. South Africa? It has Kyalami, but F1 has been trying to stage a race in Africa for some years but it proved impossible for various reasons in South Africa.

Portugal's Portimao is back on the calendar for real in 2027, but construction work needs to be done for it to be ready, and it could not do that and host a race in December.

The same goes for Istanbul Park, where the weather in December may well be no better than Imola.

And there is also all the travel-related documentation to consider.

Domenicali said last week: "Considering the constraint that we have, we need to go back to close all the Brexit-connected documentation from abroad in the UK and then go to another place.

"Therefore, the only possibility is to finish in Europe within the same framework of the time, hoping that there will be no snow, as we can hope in other places."

There seem to be more significant upgrades from a number of teams this year, McLaren's being the latest. Will the top four teams be bringing many 

All the F1 teams headed into 2026 knowing that the season would be defined by development.

When there is a new rule set, this is always the case. The longer a set of rules exists, the more a) the car designs converge; b) teams get into diminishing returns.

But at the start, progress comes faster and in bigger steps, and that explains the fluctuation in form between the top teams so far this season.

Typically, a team will bring an upgrade, their competitiveness will increase, but then it will shift as other teams bring their own upgrades.

The longer a team leaves it between upgrades, the more they fall back.

That's why McLaren, for example, made a leap forward with their Miami upgrade, but slowly slipped back as Mercedes and Ferrari brought their own big developments in Canada and Spain.

Then, McLaren leapt forwards - even more than they expected - with their Hungary upgrade. And they have another due in Zandvoort. And more to come after that.

Ferrari, Mercedes and Red Bull also have developments to come after the summer break.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said in Hungary: "I still believe that if we want to be in a position to fight for victories consistently in the future, we need to keep our focus on delivering more upgrades. That is the plan, but we are not naive. We know that this will be the plan for all the teams.

"Like it's always been in this 2026 season, it's a matter of a race of upgrades. And the good news is that McLaren is now back in this race of upgrades while fighting for the lead.

"But I expect that the car that will be the best car at the end of the season will keep adding tenths of a second in the next 11 races, probably as much as half a second. So definitely a lot of work ahead of everyone, not only McLaren."

The limiting factor is the cost cap - all teams are restricted to spending no more than $215m on racing and development this season.

This means teams have to be strategic in how they deploy their new parts, "rather than just throwing it in at every grand prix, like in the past", as Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff put it in Hungary.

He added: "We're bringing upgrades, we're closely monitoring how much we can bring. At the moment, cost cap-wise, we're in a good spot. We've tried to have it a little bit more second-half-of-the-season weighted, and we'll see if that's enough."

Why don't McLaren make their own engines? They often seem to struggle because they rely on others' (Mercedes) power units, who are also a direct competitor. Surely McLaren have the expertise and they could benefit their road car industry and their F1 car if they became a works team. - Jack

Making a Formula 1 engine is a highly specialised enterprise. It's also extremely expensive. The manufacturers supplying engines to F1 this year have all spent hundreds of millions of pounds developing their power-units.

Apart from Red Bull, all are car manufacturers who have wider automotive companies to offset the cost, and expertise on which to lean.

There is now an engine budget cap, set at $190m in a company's inaugural year, and $148.5m after that.

McLaren is a road-car manufacturer. But it does not build engines. It outsources its engines to a UK company called Ricardo.

The plans for the next F1 engine, due in either 2030 or 2031, are still being formalised, and there is considerable debate about them.

However, one aspect all stakeholders are agreed upon is for the costs to come down, perhaps even to the point where becoming a supplier of customer engines becomes a viable business proposition, which is not the case at the moment.

McLaren have proved they can win titles as a customer team, but they have also had frustrations with their Mercedes relationship this year. They have discovered how customer teams are on the back foot when it comes to maximising the operations of such complex engines at the start of a new regulation cycle.

As for the future, McLaren Racing chief executive officer Zak Brown said at the Monaco Grand Prix: "Priority one is to stay with Mercedes. They've been a great partner. Any time a new regulation comes out, we'll take a look and see, is it something technically that's interesting? Is it something fiscally that makes sense?

"We'll go through that process when that happens. But sitting here right now, we're extremely happy with Mercedes and we anticipate continuing with them."

title: Itauma v Hrgovic upgraded to IBF world-title bout
description: British heavyweight Moses Itauma's fight against Filip Hrgovic on 29 August will be for the vacant IBF title.
fullText:
British heavyweight Moses Itauma's fight against Filip Hrgovic on 29 August will be for the vacant IBF title.

Itauma, 21, has been widely tipped as the next star of heavyweight boxing, with 12 knockouts in 14 professional victories.

Promoter Frank Warren told BBC Sport the IBF belt, vacated by Oleksandr Usyk in June, will be on the line at London's O2 Arena.

"A lot of people have high expectations of him as I have, by the way," Queensberry Promotions' Warren told BBC Sport.

"We signed him when he was 16. He was an amateur. We sponsored him and he turned professional with us. And he's been amazing and sort of taken the world by storm.

"This is a big moment for him. But I'm confident he can do it."

Itauma would become the youngest heavyweight champion since Mike Tyson if he beats Hrgovic.

He had initially been ordered to enter negotiations with Cuban Frank Sanchez for the vacant title and was given a deadline of 29 July.

However, Sanchez has agreed to step aside and will instead face the winner of the bout.

"We paid [Sanchez] some money. We said whoever wins the fight, you're not losing out and you'll get the opportunity to fight for the title against the winner," Warren added.

Itauma impressed in a fifth-round stoppage of American Jermaine Franklin in Manchester in March and stopped Briton Dillian Whyte in one round in August 2025.

Hrgovic, a 2016 Olympic bronze medallist, has won 20 professional fights. The 34-year-old stopped Briton Dave Allen in the third round in May.

"We know Hrgovic is going to come and give 100%, and 100% of him is hard work for anyone," Warren said.

Nigerian heritage key to my success - Itauma

Itauma handed everything on a plate - Hrgovic

A victory for Itauma could set up an all-British unification fight next year.

WBO champion Daniel Dubois defeated Fabio Wardley in May to become a two-time heavyweight world champion, and Warren confirmed the pair will contest a rematch in October.

Warren says should Itauma beat Hrgovic and then Sanchez, a fight against Ipswich's Wardley or Londoner Dubois for two world titles may take place at Wembley Stadium in 2027.

"It would be huge, absolutely huge. They're big punchers. These guys are big, big punchers. They're exciting. They're not in boring fights," Warren said.

Wardley and Itauma are both trained by Ben Davison, and Warren says the trainer will have to "make a decision" if the fight happens.

"I've seen best friends fight each other but they do it for the money they get, which pays the bills," Warren added.

Russian Murat Gassiev is the WBA champion, while Germany's Agit Kabayel holds the WBC title and is also signed to Queensberry.

Itauma could become the second-youngest British boxer in the modern era to win a professional world title. The Chatham fighter will be 21 years and 244 days old when the fight takes place.

Prince Naseem Hamed, at 21 years and 218 days, captured a world title at a younger age when he stopped Steve Robinson to win the WBO featherweight title in 1995.

Teddy Baldock won the vacant world bantamweight title against Archie Bell in 1927, aged 19 years and 346 days.

"Obviously I'm proud of what he's done up to now but if he does this I'll be the happiest guy around because he's such a nice guy," Warren said.

"He is a great advert for British boxing, world boxing and for sport."

title: MLB Trade Grades: A’s Have Quiet Trade Deadline
description: Should the team have done more?
fullText:
While nearly every other MLB team made moves at the 2026 MLB trade deadline to boost its present and future, the Athletics sat on the sidelines, unwilling to shake up a roster that is staring down a fifth straight losing season.

Entering the deadline, it felt like the A's were not going to do much, as the organization continues building in anticipation of its 2028 relocation to Las Vegas. As such, it made sense that the team kept recently extended starters Jacob Wilson and Tyler Soderstrom off the market, as well as promising rookies Henry Bolte, Gage Jump and Joshua Kuroda-Grauer.

The reason why the team did basically nothing was that it had no healthy, valuable players to put on the trade block. Injuries and performance regression were major factors behind the team's collapse over the past couple of months.

The A's two pending free-agents, left-handed pitcher Jeffrey Springs and second baseman Jeff McNeil, stayed with the team. Their poor performances and team-options for next season likely discouraged contending teams from pursuing them.

The Athletics' lone move was announced right at the deadline. The club traded 25-year-old outfielder Colby Thomas to the Philadelphia Phillies in exchange for right-handed reliever Seth Johnson.

Thomas had plenty of opportunity to prove himself with the Athletics since he made his MLB debut last August, but he failed to provide much of an impact. With the A's, he accumulated 10 home runs and 30 RBIs over his first 234 major league at-bats. Now he goes to Philadelphia, where he will look to provide some thump against left-handed pitchers for a Phillies team in the postseason hunt.

Johnson can immediately slot into an A's bullpen in need of help. Through 16 appearances with the Phillies this season, the hard-throwing 27-year-old recorded a 1-0 record, a 5.51 ERA and 20 strikeouts. He has fared significantly better at Triple-A, going 1-1 with a 2.17 ERA at that lower level.

They traded from a position of strength, getting rid of Thomas, who projects as only a platoon bat due to the incompetence he has shown against right-handed pitchers. In return, they acquired a former highly ranked pitching prospect who could help a bullpen that owns the worst ERA in the majors

Johnson's electric arsenal consists of a high-90s four-seam fastball and a power slider. He has struggled to limit the walks, making him a natural fit for this walk-happy pitching staff. If the A's can harness his stuff and help him throw more strikes, he could emerge as a late-inning weapon for this bullpen-needy club.

The Green and Gold could have made more of an impact had starting catcher Shea Langeliers not suffered a torn meniscus. Given his multiple years of team control and elite all-around performance, Langeliers would have fetched the Athletics a return on par if not bigger than what the Boston Red Sox sent to the Baltimore Orioles in exchange for mutli-time All-Star catcher Adley Rutschman.

Unfortunately, Langeliers' potential season-ending injury took him off the market. It also likely contributed to the team keeping fellow catcher Jonah Heim, a free-agent at season's end.
